INter Apostolorum choragos, S. Paulum praeputii,& S.Petrum circumcisionis Apostolos memorabilis contentio incidit, quam ipse S.Paulus Gal.II.11--15. his verbis narrat: Ὅτε δὲ ἦλθε Πέτρος εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν, κατὰ πρόσωπον αὐτῷ ἀντέστην, ὅτι κατεγνωσμένος ἦν (v. 12.) πρὸ τοῦ γὰρ ἐλθεῖν τινας ἀπὸ Ἰακώβου μετὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν συνήσθιεν· ὅτε δὲ ἦλθον, ὑπέστελλε καὶ ἀφώριζεν ἑαυτόν, φοβούμενος τοὺς ἐκ περιτομῆς (v. 13.) καὶ συνυπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ Ἰουδαῖοι, ὥστε καὶ Βαρναβᾶς συναπήχθη[?] αὐτῶν τῇ ὑποκρίσει (v. 14.) Ἀλλ' ὅτε εἶδον, ὅτι οὐκ ὀρθοποδοῦσι[?] πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου, εἶπον τῷ Πέτρῳ ἔμπροσθεν πάντων· Εἰ σὺ Ἰουδαῖος ὑπάρχων ἐθνικῶς[?] ζῇς, καὶ οὐκ Ἰουδαϊκῶς, τί τὰ ἔθνη ἀναγκάζεις Ἰουδαΐζειν; &c. Cum autem venisset Petrus Antiochiam, in faciem ei restiti: quia damnandus erat. (v. 12.) Nam antequam venissent quidam à Jacobo, unà cum gentibus vescebatur: quum autem venissent, subducebat se & separabat, metuens eos, qui ex circumcisione erant. (v. 13.) Et simulabant cum eo reliqui etiam Judæi. Quare & Barnabas simul abreptus fuit per illorum simulationem. (v. 14.) Sed, cum viderem, eos non recto pede incedere juxta veritatem Evangelii, dixi Petro coram omnibus: Si tu, qui Judæus es, gentiliter vivis, & non Judaicè, cur gentes cogis Judaizare?
units.tr: Among the leaders of the Apostles, a memorable contention arose between St Paul, the Apostle of the uncircumcision, and St Peter, the Apostle of the circumcision. St Paul himself recounts it in Galatians 2:11–15 in these words: "But when Peter had come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be condemned (v. 12). For before certain men came from James, he ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those of the circumcision (v. 13). And the rest of the Jews dissembled with him as well, so that even Barnabas was carried away by their dissimulation (v. 14). But when I saw that they did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Peter before them all: If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do and not as the Jews, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews?" [Ὅτε δὲ ἦλθε Πέτρος εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν, κατὰ πρόσωπον αὐτῷ ἀντέστην, ὅτι κατεγνωσμένος ἦν· πρὸ τοῦ γὰρ ἐλθεῖν τινας ἀπὸ Ἰακώβου μετὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν συνήσθιεν· ὅτε δὲ ἦλθον, ὑπέστελλε καὶ ἀφώριζεν ἑαυτόν, φοβούμενος τοὺς ἐκ περιτομῆς· καὶ συνυπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ Ἰουδαῖοι, ὥστε καὶ Βαρναβᾶς συναπήχθη αὐτῶν τῇ ὑποκρίσει· Ἀλλ' ὅτε εἶδον, ὅτι οὐκ ὀρθοποδοῦσι πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου, εἶπον τῷ Πέτρῳ ἔμπροσθεν πάντων· Εἰ σὺ Ἰουδαῖος ὑπάρχων ἐθνικῶς ζῇς, καὶ οὐκ Ἰουδαϊκῶς, τί τὰ ἔθνη ἀναγκάζεις Ἰουδαΐζειν;]

units.la: II. Narratio contentionis plana est; nec ullis involuta tenebris, nisi quas partim imprudentes nonnulli, partim malarum causarum patroni, partium studio abrepti, offuderunt. Quos inter famosus ille Annalium conditor Baronius ad A. C.51. n. 31. recitatis S. Pauli verbis, sic declamare non erubuit: Siste gradum, lector: hic plane lapis est offensionis, hic petra scandali, in quam complures impegisse noscuntur &c. Et n. 34. impudenter appellat locum scabrum, quem nec Augustinus inoffenso pede pertransierit. Tali scilicet reverentia Romanenses mystae sacras literas, & earum authores prosequuntur, sicubi Oecumenico Papatui suo officere vident. Has vero tenebras loco huic offusas dispellere paucis, & dispulsis iis saluberrima fidei & vitae documenta inde promere, curae hoc nobis cordique erit. Disquirendum ergo in universum: Quis Petrus ille fuerit à S. Paulo reprehensus? Qualis fuerit reprehensio Paulina, seria an simulata? Quae denique reprehendendi S. Petri causa?
units.tr: II. The account of the contention is plain, and it is not wrapped in any darkness except that which some careless writers, and some advocates of bad causes carried away by partisan zeal, have cast over it. Among them the famous annalist Baronius, after quoting the words of St Paul at the year 51, n. 31, did not blush to declaim thus: "Halt, reader: here is plainly a stone of stumbling, here a rock of offence, against which many are known to have struck…" And at n. 34 he shamelessly calls it "a rough place, which not even Augustine passed over with an unhurt foot." Such is the reverence the Roman mystics show toward the sacred letters and their authors wherever they see them standing in the way of their Ecumenical Papacy. It will be our care and concern to dispel these shadows that have been cast over this passage, in a few words, and from the dispelled shadows to draw out the most wholesome lessons of faith and life. We must inquire, then, in general: Who was that Peter rebuked by St Paul? What sort of rebuke was Paul's, serious or feigned? And finally, what was the reason for rebuking St Peter?

units.la: III. Petrum à S. Paulo reprehensum non celebrem Apostolum, sed ex LXX. discipulorum Christi censu obscurum quempiam suisse, inconsideratè olim Clemens Alexandrinus hypotyposeon quinto, ab Eusebio Hist. Eccl. lib. I. 12. citatus, statuit; & eundem, diverso licèt animo, recens secuti Carerius, Pighius, aliique pertendunt. Et Clemens quidem ideo non Πέτρον Petrum, sed Κηφᾶ[?] Cephan, contra fidem Codicum omnium, & Græcorum etiam Patrum, legit. Sed figmentum jam olim explosit Hieronymus, negans, alium in Scriptura sciri Cepham, quàm qui modò Cephas, modò Petrus insignitur. Et tota narrationis series probat, Paulum sese comparare cum Cepha illo, quem unà cum Jacobo & Johanne inter στύλας[?] columnas Ecclesiæ v. 9. retulit. Quis verò credat, eum nominato Cepha pro Petro, statim alium quendam eodem nomine protulisse, sine differentiæ notatione ulla? Nam ne Judam quidem, fratrem Domini, uspiam Evangelistæ nominant sine nota, qua ab Iscariote discriminetur. Neque obstat silentium Lucæ de Petro Apostolo, tum quia æquè siluit de Cepha quodam Christi discipulo: tum quia multa, quæ Paulus se sustinuisse narrat, aliaque tacuit idem. Firmum ergo esto, Petrum Apostolum intelligi.
units.tr: III. Long ago Clement of Alexandria, in the fifth book of his Hypotyposes, cited by Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History I.12, rashly decided that the Peter rebuked by St Paul was not the famous Apostle but some obscure person from the number of the seventy disciples of Christ. Carerius, Pighius and others, though with a different intent, have recently followed him and maintain the same. Clement indeed read not Πέτρον (Peter) but Κηφᾶ (Cephas), against the testimony of all the manuscripts and also of the Greek Fathers. But Jerome long ago exploded this fiction, denying that any other Cephas is known in Scripture than the one who is named now Cephas, now Peter. And the whole sequence of the narrative proves that Paul compares himself with that Cephas whom he listed, along with James and John, among the pillars [στῦλοι] of the Church (v. 9). Who would believe that, having named Cephas, he at once brought forward another man with the same name, without any mark of distinction? For the Evangelists never name even Judas, the brother of the Lord, without a mark distinguishing him from Iscariot. Nor does Luke's silence about the Apostle Peter stand in the way, both because he is equally silent about a certain Cephas who was a disciple of Christ, and because the same Luke passed over many things that Paul says he endured, and other things besides. Let it therefore stand firm that the Apostle Peter is meant.

units.la: IV. Sequitur reprehensio S. Pauli, quam simulatam, non veram fuisse, olim Hieronymus, studio vindicandi & Paulum & Petrū adversus blasphemias Porphyrii, impingentis Apostolis, quòd & Petrus in fide erraverit, & Paulus Petro petulanter insultaverit; asseruit: Veram, non simulatam fuisse, contra Augustinus, epistolis aliquot cum Hieronymo contentionis serram reciprocans, sustinuit.
units.tr: IV. Next comes St Paul's rebuke, which Jerome long ago asserted was feigned and not genuine. He did so out of zeal to vindicate both Paul and Peter against the blasphemies of Porphyry, who attacked the Apostles, charging that Peter had erred in faith and that Paul had insolently insulted Peter. Augustine, on the other hand, maintained against him that the rebuke was genuine and not feigned, sending back and forth the saw of contention in several letters with Jerome.

units.la: V. Simulatam reprehensionem statuens Hieronymus, οἰκονομίαν[?] ejusmodi finxit, ut diceret, ex composito sic egisse & Paulum & Petrum, ut dissidium simularent, quod nullum erat, quò utilitati discipulorum ambo ea arte consulerent. Quia enim Judæi & gentiles ad Christum conversi utrique, de ciborum discrimine contenderant hactenus, illis discrimen manere, his sublatum esse pertendentibus; eventurum sperasse Petrum & Paulum, ut Judæi obstinatiores & ipsi cederent, ciborumque usum promiscuum esse agnoscerent, Petrus, tantus scilicet Apostolus, cum Judæis facere, & ciborum discrimen propugnare visus, se à Paulo reprehendi graviter sineret, imò reprehendenti ultro concederet, victásque manus daret. Quasi scilicet ita cum Judæis infirmioribus egisset S. Paulus, sicut cum Corinthiis egisse videri poterat 2. Cor.XII.16. ubi ad Pseudapostolorum criminationem alludens scribit: Esto verò ὑπάρχων[?] πανοῦργ[?]ος δόλῳ ὑμᾶς ἔλαβον. Cùm esset astutus, dolo vos cepi.
units.tr: V. Jerome, holding that the rebuke was feigned, devised a kind of economy, namely that Paul and Peter had acted by agreement, pretending a disagreement which did not exist, so that both might serve the advantage of the disciples by this stratagem. For since the Jews and the Gentiles who had been converted to Christ had contended until then about the distinction of foods, the one party maintaining that the distinction remained, the other that it had been abolished, Paul and Peter were supposed to have hoped that the more obstinate Jews would themselves give way and acknowledge that the use of all foods was common. Peter, that great Apostle, was to seem to side with the Jews and to defend the distinction of foods, and to allow himself to be severely rebuked by Paul; indeed he would even yield to the rebuker of his own accord and give up the contest. As if, forsooth, St Paul had dealt with the weaker Jews in the way he could seem to have dealt with the Corinthians, alluding to the accusation of the false apostles, when he writes in 2 Corinthians 12:16: "But being crafty, I caught you with guile." [Ἀλλὰ ὑπάρχων πανοῦργος δόλῳ ὑμᾶς ἔλαβον.]

units.la: VI. Oeconomiæ hujus argumentum hoc inprimis Hieronymus, eúmque secuti alii urgebant, quòd S. Paulus v. 11. dicat: Κατὰ πρόσωπον αὐτῷ ἀντέστην [?] in speciem (sic illi reddunt) Petro restiti. Non ergo verè, sed simulatè. Idque v. 13. aperte innui ajunt, ubi dicitur: Συνυπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ Ἰουδαῖοι· Simulabant cum eo etiam reliqui Judæi, adeò ut etiam Barnabas simul abreptus fuerit per eorum simulationem, quasi unà cum Petro simulaverint separationem à gentilibus, hoc est, separatione ea prudens & officiosum consilium, cujus eosdem conscios & approbatores Petrus habuerit, occultaverint. Neq; putárunt illi ullum Petro peccatum impingi jure potuisse, sive in convictu cum gentilibus, quia ex libertate Christiana & absque scandalo convivere, & cibis promiscuis unâ cum iis vesci potuerit: sive in separatione à gentilibus, quia scandalum Judæorum merito & timuerit & caverit, juxta regulam ipsius Pauli: Si esca offendat fratrem meum, in æternum non vescar carnibus, 1.Cor.VIII. 13. Paria sentientes secum Origenem, Didymum, Apollinarem, Eusebium, Emisenum, Theodorum Heracleotem Hieronymus induxit. Et in eandem sententiam Chrysostomus in Epist. ad Gal. cap.II. Theodoretus ibid. Cassianus Collat. 17. Theophylactus & Oecumenius in cap. 2. ad Gal. abierunt.
units.tr: VI. Jerome, and others who followed him, pressed this argument for the economy above all, namely that St Paul says in v. 11: "I withstood him to the face" (in speciem, as they render it), that is, I withstood Peter in appearance only. Therefore it was not genuine but feigned. They say this is plainly hinted at in v. 13, where it is said: "And the rest of the Jews dissembled with him as well, so that even Barnabas was carried away by their dissimulation" [Συνυπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ Ἰουδαῖοι], as if the other Jews had feigned separation from the Gentiles along with Peter, and had concealed by that separation a prudent and dutiful plan, of which Peter would have had them as accomplices and approvers. Nor did they think that any fault could rightly be charged against Peter, either in his fellowship with the Gentiles, since by Christian liberty he could eat with them without offence and share with them in common foods; or in his separation from the Gentiles, since he rightly feared and guarded against the offence of the Jews, according to the very rule of Paul: "If food offends my brother, I will never eat meat for ever," 1 Corinthians 8:13. Jerome brought in Origen, Didymus, Apollinaris, Eusebius, Eusebius of Emesa and Theodore of Heraclea as holding the same opinion with him. Chrysostom in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 2, Theodoret in the same place, Cassian in Conference 17, and Theophylact and Oecumenius on Galatians 2 went over to the same view.

units.la: VII. Vehementer huic sententiæ S. Augustinus Epist. 8. 9. 12. 15. se opposuit, eo potissimum argumento fretus, quòd nullum ab Apostolo ad Galatas scribente compositum fuerit mendacium, nec Apostolo licuerit mentiri: sicut nec cuiquam Christiano etiam officiosè mentiri fas sit. secus atque Pelagiani eodem Augustini tempore officiosa mendacia asserere, & Pauli testimonio roborare ausi sunt. Inprimis cùm S. Paulus Gal. I. 20. tam sanctè dejeraverit: Quæ scribo vobis, ecce in conspectu Dei, ἐν ὃ ψεύδομαι [?], quia non mentior. Admisso autem semel, ita Augustinus Epist. 8. arguit, in tantum authoritatis fastigium officioso aliquo mendacio, nulla illorum librorum particula remanebit, quæ non, utcunque videbitur vel ad mores difficilis, vel ad fidem incredibilis, eadem perniciosissima regula ad mentientis authoris consilium officiúmque referatur. Si enim mentiebatur Apostolus Paulus, cùm Apostolum Petrum objurgans diceret: Si tu cùm sis Judæus, gentiliter & non Judaicè vivis, quemadmodum gentes cogis Judaizare? & rectè illi videbatur Petrus fecisse, quem non rectè fecisse & dixit, & scripsit, ut quasi animos tumultuantium delinieret: quid respondebimus, cùm exstiterint perversi homines, prohibentes nuptias, quos ipse futuros prænuntiavit, & dixerint, totum illud, quod idem Apostolus de matrimoniorum jure firmando locutus est, propter homines, qui dilectione conjugum tumultuari poterant, fuisse mentitum; scilicet non quod hoc senserit, sed ut illorum placaretur adversitas?
units.tr: VII. St Augustine, in Epistles 8, 9, 12 and 15, set himself strongly against this opinion, relying chiefly on the argument that no falsehood was put forward by the Apostle writing to the Galatians, and that it was not lawful for the Apostle to lie, just as it is not right for any Christian to lie, even for a dutiful purpose. This was in contrast to the Pelagians, who in Augustine's own time dared to assert dutiful lies and to confirm them by the testimony of Paul. Above all, since St Paul swore so solemnly in Galatians 1:20: "What I write to you, behold, before God, ἐν ὃ ψεύδομαι, I do not lie." Augustine argues in Epistle 8: "Once a lie told for some dutiful purpose is admitted, not a single particle of those books will remain at the height of such authority which will not, however difficult it may seem in morals or incredible in faith, be referred by this most pernicious rule to the purpose and dutiful intention of an author who lies. For if the Apostle Paul lied, when rebuking the Apostle Peter he said: 'If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles and not as the Jews, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews?', and if Peter seemed to have acted rightly, though he said and wrote that he had not acted rightly, in order to soothe the minds of those who were in an uproar, what shall we answer when there have arisen perverse men forbidding marriage, whom he himself foretold would come, and who say that all that same Apostle said about the authority of marriage was a lie told on account of men who might be stirred to an uproar by love of their spouses; namely, not because he thought so, but so that their hostility might be calmed?"

units.la: VIII. Sic plane S. Augustino tum scribere rem secus, quam est, vel esse putatur; hoc est, scribere Paulum, se restitisse Petro, quia damnandus erat, & Petrum Judaizasse, sine ulla simulationis suae mentione, cum tamen se restitisse Petro, eumque damnasse, & eum Judaizasse per simulationem, putaret: tum verbis resistere, damnare, & facto aliquo Judaizare, nec tamen animo resistere, damnare, Judaizare, idem visum est, quod mentiri, & quidem officiose, ad lucrandos scilicet Judaeos. Nec immerito, quia sic aeque parum verba S. Pauli, sive rem factam scribentis, sive cum Petro contendentis, ac facta Petri, utriusque animo & factis congruissent. Neq; adeo[?] minueretur hypocrisis, sed duplicaretur, & fieret simulatio simulationis; hoc est, & in contentione ipsa histrionia mera, tantis Apostolis indigna: & in descriptione histrioniae hujus mendacium notorium. Etenim si apud Judaeos Hierosolymitanos Antiochiae haec simulavit Paulus, quid attinebat etiam composito mendacio simulare apud Galatas & nos, in quorum gratiam contentionem illam scripsit? An sic probasset Paulus, quod probandum susceperat v.6. Ab iis, qui existimantur esse aliquid, (quos inter Petrum nominat) nihil mihi differt. Faciem Deus non accipit? Et cui bono composita illa simulatio sive in scribendo, sive in loquendo, sive in faciendo? Cur non aperiret Petrus veritatem liberè? An plus credidissent Judaei Paulo objurganti, quam Petro docenti? Cur Paulus non Galatis consensum Petri in eadem veritate explicare, quam fictam reprehensionem pro vera iis obtrudere potius duxisset?
units.tr: VIII. Augustine plainly thought that Paul wrote otherwise than the facts were, or were thought to be. That is, he held that Paul wrote that he had resisted Peter because Peter deserved condemnation, and that Peter had judaized, with no mention of Paul's own pretence, though Paul had in fact resisted Peter and condemned him, and Peter had judaized only in pretence. To Augustine, resisting, condemning and judaizing in act but not in intention seemed to be the same as lying, and indeed lying out of kindness, namely to win the Jews. Not unreasonably, for on that view Paul's words, whether describing the event or contending with Peter, and Peter's conduct, would have agreed with neither man's mind or deeds. Hypocrisy would not be lessened but doubled, becoming a pretence of pretence: in the dispute itself, pure play-acting unworthy of such Apostles, and in the account of that play-acting, a notorious lie. For if Paul made this pretence before the Jerusalem men at Antioch, why was it also necessary to pretend, with a deliberate lie, before the Galatians and us, for whose benefit he wrote that dispute? Would Paul have proved what he had undertaken to prove in verse 6, from those who seem to be something (among whom he names Peter), it makes no difference to me; God does not accept a man's face, in this way? And what was the purpose of that composed pretence, whether in writing, in speaking or in acting? Why should Peter not have declared the truth freely? Would the Jews have believed Paul rebuking more than Peter teaching? Why would Paul rather have set forth to the Galatians Peter's agreement in the same truth than have forced upon them a feigned rebuke as if it were real?

units.la: IX. Parùm pie, certè falsò Baronius ad A.51. n.37. Augustino inscitiae & detortae sententiae Hieronymianae dicam impingit. Hieronymus enim, inquit, non hoc dicebat, Paulum esse mentitum, & ad Galatas scripsisse mendacia: quod tunc contigisset, si quae minime facta essent, ea perinde ac facta scripsisset, vel aliter quam gesta fuissent, quorum neutrum Hieronymus impingit Apostolo: sed ipsum, quae vere facta, & ut facta essent, scripsisse, nullatenus dubitavit. At longe aliud est, a Paulo vere fuisse narrata: aliud ea, quae sunt vere narrata, per simulationem ex composito facta. quod Hieronymus, & alii affirmabant authores. quod absque peccati scrupulo facere licuisse, exemplo Domini comprobarunt.
units.tr: IX. Baronius, ad A.51. n.37., has, with little piety and certainly falsely, charged Augustine with ignorance and with twisting Jerome's opinion. For Jerome, he says, did not say that Paul lied and wrote falsehoods to the Galatians. That would have happened if he had written things that had not happened as though they had, or otherwise than they were done. Jerome charges the Apostle with neither of these, but he never doubted that Paul wrote what had truly happened, and as it had happened. But it is quite another thing for things to have been truly related by Paul, and another for things that were truly related to have been done by pretence and by prior arrangement. Jerome and other authors affirmed this, and they showed by the example of the Lord that it could be done without any scruple of sin.

units.la: X. Caeterùm Baronio longè certè oculatior Augustinus fuit. Nam argumento hoc, quòd sic Apostoli mentiti essent, Hieronymi jugulum petit, nec rectius petere potuisset. Posita enim Hieronymi opinione, quòd contentio & objurgatio Paulina tota simulata & composita fuerit, optimè Augustinus arguit, mendacium in Scriptura reperiri. Paulus enim v. 11. 14. scribit, se in facie, restitisse Petro, quia damnari debuerit, & viderit, quòd non incesserit recto pede juxta veritatem Evangelii. Hoc totum utique per mendacium diceretur. Resistere enim & damnare notat contentionem & contrarium nixum: damnabilem esse, notat praevium errorem vel peccatum: non incedere recto pede juxta veritatem Evangelii, notat declinationem à veritate Evangelii. Si ergo S. Paulus non verè, sed per simulationem reprehendit, damnavit Petrum innocentem: si Petrus non erravit, non declinavit à veritate Evangelii, Paulus ergo scribens, se Petro restitisse, & vidisse, quòd non recto pede incesserit juxta veritatem Evangelii; adeóque innuens, Petrum reum fuisse, peccâsse, se videnté à veritate declinâsse, cùm revera necdamnatus, nec reus fuerit, nec peccaverit, nec declinaverit à veritate Evangelii, nisi per simulationem, cujus tamen mentionem describendo resistentiae historiam nullam aspersit, utique mendacio historiam suam polluit, veritatis lineas transfiliit. Nam non narrare rem, uti est, sed secus atque est, mentiri est. Ita si pictum hominem ostentes, ea adhibita arte & solertia, eo animo, ut deceptus alter verum hominem esse existimet, fallis certè & mentiris evidenter. Quorsum enim Galatis talia commemoravit S. Paulus? Annon ut à legalibus eos avocaret: atque ita avocaret, ut contrarium etiam Petri Judaizantis exemplum a parte perstringeret? Si contrarium non fuit, nec verè perstrinxit, certè a mendacio excusari nequit, innuens, contrarium fuisse, & ideo á se perstrictum, nec simulata haec, non ex animo gesta esse, commemorans. Qua etiam narratione simplici injuriam S. Petro manifestè fecisset, hunc in animo lectoris aculeū relinquens, quasi damnandus fuisset, Judaizâsset, à veritate Evangelii declinâsset. Nam per simulationem sic se Petrū reprehendisse, non meminit. Licet ergo Hieronymus nec dixerit, nec agnoverit, Paulum mentitum esse; tamen ex Hieronymi opinione Augustinus consequi pertendit, Paulum contraria factis scribentem, nec facta sua simulata esse, insinuantem, mentiturum fuisse. Cùm igitur à Spiritu Dei inspiratus mentiri non potuerit, contraria factis non scripsisse, adeóque contentionem verissimam fuisse, sapientissimè arguit.
units.tr: X. Augustine, however, was certainly far sharper-sighted than Baronius. For by this argument, that the Apostles lied in this way, he attacks Jerome's throat, and he could not have attacked it more rightly. For on Jerome's opinion, that Paul's contention and rebuke were wholly feigned and arranged, Augustine rightly argues that a lie is found in Scripture. Paul writes at verses 11 and 14 that he resisted Peter to his face, because he ought to be condemned, and he saw that he did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel. All this would surely be said by a lie. For to resist and to condemn denote contention and opposing effort; to be blameworthy denotes a prior error or sin; not to walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel denotes a departure from the truth of the Gospel. If then St Paul did not rebuke and condemn truly but by pretence, he condemned an innocent man. If Peter did not err or depart from the truth of the Gospel, then Paul, writing that he resisted Peter and saw that he did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, and so implying that Peter was guilty, had sinned, and had departed from the truth in his sight, when in fact Peter was neither condemned, nor guilty, nor sinful, nor departed from the truth of the Gospel, except by pretence, of which Paul, in describing the history of the resistance, made no mention. Paul would then have stained his history with a lie and leapt over the lines of truth. For to relate a thing not as it is, but otherwise than it is, is to lie. So if you display a painted man, with such art and skill, and with the intention that the other, deceived, should think him a real man, you clearly deceive and lie. For why did St Paul recount such things to the Galatians? Was it not to turn them away from the legalists? And to turn them away in such a way that he also, in part, censured the contrary example of Peter judaizing? If it was not contrary, and he did not truly censure it, he certainly cannot be excused from lying, since he implies that it was contrary and was therefore censured by him, and he does not mention that these things were done in pretence and not from the heart. By this plain narrative he would have done manifest injury to St Peter, leaving in the reader's mind a sting as though Peter deserved condemnation, had judaized, and had departed from the truth of the Gospel. For he does not mention that he rebuked Peter in this way by pretence. Therefore, although Jerome neither said nor acknowledged that Paul lied, Augustine nevertheless maintains that on Jerome's opinion it follows that Paul, writing things contrary to his deeds, and hinting that his deeds were not feigned, would have lied. Since, then, Paul, inspired by the Spirit of God, could not lie, and did not write things contrary to his deeds, Augustine rightly and very wisely argues that the contention was entirely true.

units.la: XI. S. Paulus Petro (v.11.) restitit: & restitit κατὰ πρόσωπον[?] in faciem; hoc est, palàm, (v.14.) ἐνώπιον[?] πάντων coram omnibus: quomodo publicè peccantes redarguendos esse, ipsemet 1. Tim. V.20. monet: adeóque non sola externa specie, uti Hieronymo visum (nusquam enim κατὰ πρόσωπον[?] simulationem, fictionem, semper rem, quae geritur in praesentia, Scriptoribus sacris significat) & sic restitit, quia καταγνωσμένος[?] ἦν damnabilis erat; non, quia damnatus, ab iis scilicet, qui facto Petri offendebantur, ignari, quid dispensative hoc est, latente consilio, ageretur. uti rursus Hieronymus detorquet. Nam καταγνωσμένος[?] idem est quod καταγνώστης[?], qui reprehensione dignus est: & opponitur Tit. II. 8. ἀκαταγνώστως[?], ei, qui jure reprehendi, damnari nequit. Quomodo aliàs constaret ratio: Restiti ei, quia damnatus est ab aliis? Neque enim temeraria aliorum damnatio argumentum resistendi Paulo esse debuit, vel potuit. Imò historia ipsa reclamat. Judaei enim cum eo in simulationem abrepti fuerunt. Non ergo eum reprehenderunt, damnârunt. Nec gentiles conversos Petrum damnâsse legimus. Sed dignus planè erat Petrus, qui damnaretur à S. Paulo, vel eam ob causam, quòd prior ipse suum factum damnavit, cùm diceret: Quid tentatis Deum, jugum (cujus pars erat lex de discrimine ciborum) imponendo discipulis Act. X. 10?
units.tr: XI. St Paul resisted Peter (v. 11), and he resisted to his face [κατὰ πρόσωπον]; that is, openly, (v. 14) before all [ἐνώπιον πάντων]. In 1 Timothy 5:20 he himself advises that those who sin publicly must be rebuked publicly. Therefore he did not resist only in outward appearance, as it seemed to Jerome (for the sacred writers nowhere use to his face [κατὰ πρόσωπον] to signify pretence or fiction, but always a thing done in the presence of others). And he resisted because he was condemnable [καταγνωσμένος ἦν, he was blameworthy], not because he had been condemned by those, that is, who were offended by Peter's action and did not know what was being done dispensatively, that is, with a hidden purpose, as Jerome again twists it. For καταγνωσμένος means the same as καταγνώστης [blameworthy], one who deserves rebuke; and in Titus 2:8 it is opposed to ἀκαταγνώστως [irreproachably], that is, to one who cannot rightly be rebuked or condemned. Otherwise how would the reasoning stand: I resisted him because he had been condemned by others? For the rash condemnation of others ought not to have been, nor could have been, the reason for Paul's resistance. Indeed the history itself protests against it. For the Jews were carried away with him into the pretence; so they did not rebuke or condemn him. Nor do we read that the Gentile converts condemned Peter. But Peter was plainly worthy to be condemned by St Paul, if only for this reason, that he had himself condemned his own action beforehand, when he said: Why do you tempt God, by putting a yoke (of which the law about the distinction of foods was a part) on the disciples? (Acts 10:10).

units.la: XII. Seriam ergo, non simulatam fuisse contentionem, ipse etiam Baronius agnoscit. Sed, mirum dictu, novo, de quo ipse gloriatur, invento, Petrum à Paulo reprehensum, damnatum licet, innocentem fuisse, pertendit. Et, quae protervia viri est, non veretur ad A. 51. n. 34. scribere, Augustinum, illum verticem Theologorum, à linea Catholica fidei aberrâsse, dum de Bapt. contra Donat. lib. II. 1. exemplo Petri Cyprianum errantem excusans, Petrum in crimen adducit. Infra autem n.39. sic idem scribit: Cùm authores omnes in alterutram sententiam conspirárint, atque in eo convenerint, vel ea cuncta esse simulatè peracta, ac sic nullum fuisse Petri peccatum; vel seriò esse facta, ac sic Petrum erràsse, nos neutram harum sequentes, dicimus, ea nec ex composito facta, nec ea faciendo Petrum vel (NB) minimùm deliquisse. Atque hic longam pariter & perplexam instituit disputationem, cujus summa huc redit: Potuisse Apostolos uti legalibus absque ulla vel levissima culpa secundum loci & temporis rationem. Jam verò & loci & temporis rationem postulasse, ut legalibus tunc uteretur Petrus, quia vitandum illi erat scandalum Judaeorum, qui Hierosolymis venerant, quorum patrocinium suscepe-rat[?]; quique magnas turbas excitaturi fuissent, si non tantùm illis non fuisset concessum in Gentiles legalia propagari, sed etiam ipsi Judaei penitus legalibus spoliarentur, & ad gentilitatem redigerentur. Reprehensum vero eundem fuisse à Paulo, cùm Judaizantem, & non recto pede incedentem juxta veritatem Evangelii, non quòd peccasset, vel imprudenter etiam egisset, sed quia ejus actio & simulatio rationabili causa usurpata, præter ejus intentionem, spem & sententiam occasionem præbuerit, ut etiam gentiles, ac eorum doctor Barnabas, tanti Apostoli exemplo & authoritate freti, judaizarent. A quo peccato immunis adeò fuerit Petrus, ut etiam apud gentiles solos versatus gentiliter vixerit. Hactenus ille. Cui secundas facit Nicolaus Abramus, S. J. in Universitate Mussiponti, de Mendacio ac veritate lib. IV. ii. ubi simulasse Petrum ait abusive, secundum communiorem illam simulationis notionem, non ab agentis intentione, sed ab eventu, qui actionem excepit; non quòd aliquid falsò significaverit, sed quòd eum intuentes aliter ejus factum acceperint, itaque fuerint interpretati, quasi legis antiquæ ceremonias Christianis omnibus necessarias judicaret. Quo factum est, inquit, ut etiam Christiani gentiles non jubentis imperio, sed authoritatis exemplo Judaizare cogerentur, multique adeò, qui legis Judaicæ jugum tolerabile non putabant, se à Christianis sacris averterent.
units.tr: XII. Even Baronius himself acknowledges that the contention was earnest and not feigned. But, strange to say, by a novelty of which he himself boasts, he maintains that Peter, though rebuked and condemned by Paul, was innocent. And, what boldness the man has, he does not hesitate to write, ad A. 51. n. 34., that Augustine, that summit of theologians, strayed from the Catholic line of faith, when in On Baptism against the Donatists, Book II, chapter 1, excusing Cyprian's error by the example of Peter, he brings Peter into guilt. Further on, at n. 39, he writes thus: Since all the authors have agreed on one or the other view, and have agreed that either all this was done by pretence, and so Peter had no sin; or it was done seriously, and so Peter erred; we, following neither of these, say that these things were done neither by prior arrangement nor by doing them did Peter commit even the least fault (NB). And here he sets out a long and tangled disputation, the sum of which comes to this: The Apostles could use the legal observances without any, even the slightest, fault, according to the reasons of place and time. Now indeed the reason of place and time required that Peter should use the legal observances then, because he had to avoid offending the Jews who had come to Jerusalem, whose patronage he had undertaken, and who would have stirred up great disturbances if it had not only been refused them to spread legal practices among the Gentiles, but also if the Jews themselves had been wholly stripped of the law and reduced to the status of Gentiles. But that Peter was rebuked by Paul, when he judaized and did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, was not because he had sinned, or even acted imprudently, but because his action and pretence, adopted for a reasonable cause, beyond his intention, hope and opinion, gave occasion that even the Gentiles, and their teacher Barnabas, relying on the example and authority of so great an Apostle, should judaize. Peter was so free from this sin that, even while living among Gentiles only, he lived as a Gentile. So far he. Nicolaus Abramus, of the Society of Jesus, at the University of Pont-à-Mousson, On Lying and Truth, Book IV, chapter 2, comes second to him. There he says that Peter pretended in an abusive sense, according to the more common notion of pretence, not from the intention of the agent but from the outcome that followed the action; not because he signified anything falsely, but because those who observed him took his action otherwise, and so interpreted it as though he judged the ceremonies of the old law necessary for all Christians. Hence it came about, he says, that even Gentile Christians were compelled to judaize, not by a command but by the example of authority, and many who did not think the yoke of the Jewish law bearable turned away from Christian worship.

units.la: XIII. Tanti erat cavere Capitolino Jovi, ne ex reprehensione & peccato Petri non tam principatui ejus, quàm Papæ vulnus infligeretur. Nil pensi habent homines hi S. Paulo injustitiæ labem aspergere, dum S. Petrus immunis exeat, & ea immunitas Papæ Monarchiam protegat. Dicite ergo, nova Papatus lumina, quis jure in os restitit ei: quis jure damnavit eum, qui omnis culpæ vacuus est? Cujus facto pio, prudente, ἀκαταγνώσῳ & inculpabili penitus, abusi sunt alii minùs piè, minùs prudenter, minùs culpabiliter? Quis sine culpa sua ὑποκρίσεως hypocriseos (cujus S. Paulus Petrum, Barnabam & alios reos fuisse v. 13. pronuntiat) reus peractus unquam fuit? Quis sine culpa sua δειλὸς meticulosus, timidus, qualem fuisse Petrum idem S. Paulus v. 12. asserit? Quis sine peccato non recto pede juxta veritatem Evangelii incedit, & Christianos, libertatis per Christum partæ compotes Judaicè vivere, hoc est, jugum Judæis olim impositum suscipere, atque sic (Act. XV. 10.) Deum tentare cogit? Annon summa iniquitas S. Pauli fuisset, Petro propter culpam simpliciter alienam, nullo modo propriam, in os re-sistere, eum damnare, ceu timidum, simulantem, non incedentem recto pede juxta veritatem Evangelii, liberos & liberatos per Christum ad Judaismum cogentem?
units.tr: XIII. So much was it worth to guard against the Capitoline Jove, lest through Peter's rebuke and sin the wound fall not so much on his primacy as on the Pope's. These men care nothing for splashing a stain of injustice on St Paul, provided St Peter comes out unscathed and that immunity shields the Papal monarchy. Tell me then, you new lights of the Papacy: who had the right to resist him to his face? Who had the right to condemn the one who was free of all fault? By whose deed, pious, prudent, utterly blameless [ἀκαταγνώσῳ] and irreproachable, did others abuse it, less piously, less prudently, less blamelessly? Who was ever convicted of hypocrisy [ὑποκρίσεως] without fault of his own (St Paul pronounces Peter, Barnabas and the others guilty of it, v. 13)? Who was ever timid [δειλὸς], fearful, as St Paul asserts Peter was in v. 12, without sin? Who, without sin, does not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, and compels Christians, made partakers of freedom through Christ, to live as Jews, that is, to take up the yoke once laid on the Jews, and so (Acts 15:10) to tempt God? Would it not have been the greatest injustice on St Paul's part to resist him to his face over a fault that was simply another's and in no way Peter's own, to condemn him as timid, dissembling, not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, compelling to Judaism those who are free and freed through Christ?

units.la: XIV. Certum quidem est, potuisse eo tempore Apostolos Judaicis ritibus liberè uti, cùm nondum abjecta, sepulta Judaica Synagoga essèt; loci scilicet, temporis, personarum ratione prudenter habita. Sed Petrum loci, temporis, personarum rationem prudenter habuisse, qui cognoscere potuerunt novi hi Doctores magis quàm Paulus? Etenim Paulus tum aderat Antiochiæ: videbat, cognoscebat, numerabat personas tunc præsentes, sive è gentibus, sive è Judæis: sciebat, quando id fiebat, ante, an post Concilium Hierosolymitanum, quo sancitum fuerat, ne discipulis jugum imponeretur, factum sit: Petrum & familiariter jam noverat, & dilexerat coluerátque, ceu columnam Ecclesiæ; & tamen eum peccasse pronuntiat. Contra mus[?]tei hi doctores, sedecim seculis post id tempus nati, nunquam fuerunt Antiochiæ, sed cùm hæc commentarentur, vel Romæ, vel Mussiponti: earum personarum, quæ tum aderant, & quarum ratio habenda fuit, nullam unquam viderunt, nec numerum iniverunt; denique eorum omnium nihil noverunt, nisi quantum à S. Paulo didicerunt. Et tamen ferrea fronte pronuntiant, in Petrum nullam delicti suspicionem cadere. Hoccine, an illud, certius, justius judicium putabimus?
units.tr: XIV. It is certainly true that at that time the Apostles could use Jewish rites freely, since the Jewish synagogue had not yet been cast off and buried; that is, with place, time and persons prudently taken into account. But who could know better than Paul whether Peter had taken account of place, time and persons prudently? For Paul was then present at Antioch. He saw, he knew, he counted the persons then present, whether from the Gentiles or from the Jews. He knew when this happened, whether before or after the Council of Jerusalem, at which it had been decreed that the disciples should not be burdened with a yoke. He had already come to know Peter intimately, and had loved and esteemed him as a pillar of the Church; and yet he pronounces that he sinned. On the other hand, these teachers, born sixteen centuries after that time, were never at Antioch, but were writing these things either at Rome or at Mussipont. They never saw the persons who were then present, whose circumstances ought to have been considered, nor did they take any count of them; in short, they knew nothing of all these things except what they had learned from St Paul. And yet they declare with brazen face that no suspicion of fault can fall upon Peter. Which judgement shall we think more certain and more just: this one, or that one?

units.la: XV. Fuit sanè S. Petrus Judæorum Apostolus. Eorum præcipuè rationem habere debuit. licet non ita eorum patronus , & protectòr,uti Ordinibus Monachorum in Papatu Cardinales certi patroni & protectores dantur. quod voce patroni adhibita somniasse Baronius videtur. Docere enim Judæos, non protegere debuit. Sed de hoc quicquid sit,certè Petrus non omnino nullam rationem habere debuit gentilium, tum inprimis, cùm non in Judæa, sed extra Judæam Antiochiæ inter gentiles Græcos, numero Judæis advenis Hierosolyma,adeóq; per accidens Antiochiæ versantibus, longè potiores hæsit. Quidni ergo sicut Paulus Judæis factus est ut Judæus, gentiũ licet Apostolus: ita Petrus, Judæorũ Apostolus licet,ἀνόμοις ὡς ἀνομῷ [?] exlegibus,sicut exlex, adeóq; omnia omnibus fieri pariter debuit, ut aliquos eorũ lucraretur,salvaret,1.Cor.IX.20.21? Non enim Apostoli partium studio abripi, vel partes seu facere seu sequi debuerunt. Unde Petrus ipse in Concilio Hierosolymitano Act. XV.7. 8. &c. gentilium causæ impensè adeò favit, ut eos, qui jugum illis imponere, hoc est, eos ad Judaizandum cogere voluerunt, Deum tentare palam edixerit. Et quæ tandem Judæis scandali causa fuit? An quòd non tantùm gentilibus jugum legis non imponeretur, sed etiam Judæis auferretur, uti Baronius prætexit? Atqui id ipsum erant docendi, ceu confor-me me Apostolico decreto, ut libertate uti, non offendi assuescerent. Neque plus inde periculi a Petro, quàm a Paulo, quia etiam hic Judæus erat, & gentiliter vivebat. Denique qui fieri potuit, ut majus periculum glisceret a facto Petri, quàm a facto Pauli, Petrum justum scilicet & innocentem ob alienum facinus reprehendentis, imò damnantis? Ita non tam amore Petri, seu potius Papalis Monarchiæ Petrü fullones hi purgant, si purgant, quàm furore cœci Paulum damnant.
units.tr: XV. St Peter was indeed the Apostle of the Jews, and he ought especially to have regarded them, though not as their patron and protector, as in the Papacy certain cardinals are given as patrons and protectors to the orders of monks. Baronius seems to have dreamed this up by using the word patron. For he ought to teach the Jews, not to protect them. But whatever the case with this, certainly Peter ought not to have had no regard at all for the Gentiles, especially since he was not in Judea but outside it, at Antioch, among Greek Gentiles, who far outnumbered the Jewish sojourners from Jerusalem, and who were there only by chance. Why then, just as Paul became as a Jew to the Jews, though he was the Apostle of the Gentiles, should Peter not likewise, though he was the Apostle of the Jews, become as one without law to those without law [ἀνόμοις ὡς ἀνομῷ], and so become all things to all men, in order to gain and save some of them (1 Cor. 9:20, 21)? For Apostles ought not to be swept away by zeal for a party, nor to make or follow parties. Hence Peter himself, at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15:7, 8, &c.), so favoured the cause of the Gentiles that he openly declared that those who wished to impose a yoke on them, that is, to compel them to Judaize, were tempting God. And what, in the end, was the cause of offence to the Jews? Was it that the yoke of the law was not imposed on the Gentiles only, but was also taken away from the Jews, as Baronius pretends? But this very thing was what they had to be taught: that, in accordance with the Apostolic decree, they should grow accustomed to use their liberty without taking offence. Nor was there more danger from Peter than from Paul, since Paul too was a Jew and lived as a Gentile. Finally, how could it come about that a greater danger should arise from Peter's deed than from Paul's, when Peter, forsooth just and innocent, was rebuking, indeed condemning, another's crime? So these fullers of Peter cleanse (if they do cleanse) not so much out of love for Peter, or rather for the Papal monarchy of Peter, as they condemn Paul out of blind fury.

units.la: XVI. Nequicquam verò ad asylum bonæ intentionis Petri ejusdem promachi confugiunt. Non enim malum facere licet, ut bonum eveniat, Rom. III. 8. Et bonum opus, uti scitè Augustinus in Psal. 31. loquitur, intentio facit, intentionem fides dirigit. Non potuit autem hypocrisis, declinatio à veritate Evangelii, coactio ad Judaizandum, propter quam Petrus damnandus fuit, in fide fieri, adeóque nec intentionem dirigere. Intentio autem per fidem non directa nec bonum opus facit, nec malum excusat, præsertim in materia scandali. Scandalum enim, quod Thoma 2. 2. q. 43. art. definiente, est dictum vel factum minus rectum, præbens occasionem ruinæ, non tantum illud est, cùm quis directè intendit ruinam proximi, & operatur aliquid minùs rectè, cujus occasione proximus labitur: sed etiam, cùm quis, non intendens peccatum alterius, facit opus vel verè, vel apparenter malum, ex quo scit, aut scire debet consecuturam ruinam proximi, quod veri nominis scandalum, & interpretativè voluntarium etiam, dici solet. Opus porro nostrum quoties sive natura sua, sive ex ascititia circumstantia proximum ad peccatum inducit, vel inducere aptum natum est, sive effectus sequatur, sive non sequatur, malum haud dubiè, & tum peccatum proprium, tum peccati alieni illecebra est. Tale autem Petri fuisse, tum inde colligitur, quia condemnari debuit: tum ex re ipsa liquidò constat.
units.tr: XVI. In vain, however, do they flee to the refuge of the good intention of that same champion of Peter. For one may not do evil that good may come (Rom. 3:8). And a good work, as Augustine well says in Ps. 31, intention makes it, faith directs the intention. But the hypocrisy, the departure from the truth of the Gospel, the compulsion to Judaize, for which Peter was to be condemned, could not be done in faith, and so could not direct the intention. An intention not directed by faith makes neither a good work nor excuses an evil one, especially in a matter of scandal. For scandal, which Thomas (2. 2. q. 43. art.) defines as a deed or word less right, presenting an occasion of ruin, is not only the case when someone directly intends the ruin of his neighbour and does something less rightly, by which occasion the neighbour falls; it is also the case when someone, not intending another's sin, does a work that is truly or apparently evil, knowing, or being bound to know, that the neighbour's ruin will follow from it. This is commonly called scandal in the proper sense, and also interpretatively voluntary. Moreover, whenever our work, whether by its own nature or by an added circumstance, leads the neighbour into sin, or is naturally apt to lead him there, whether or not the effect follows, it is undoubtedly evil, and it is both one's own sin and an enticement to another's sin. That Peter's act was of this kind is gathered both from the fact that he ought to have been condemned, and from the matter itself, which plainly appears.

units.la: XVII. Etenim S. Petrus Antiochiæ, priùs quàm Judæi Hierosolyma à Jacobo missi advenissent, μετὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν συνῇσθιε una cum gentibus vescebatur, gnarus scilicet, ciborum nullum amplius discrimen religionis gratia vigere, quosque cibos Deus purificavit, illos pro impuris amplius habendos non esse, Act. X.15. & discipulis, hoc est, proselythis[?] gentium, jugum, cujus pars erat lex cibaria à Mose imperata, imponendum non esse, Act. XV. 10.28. Hactenus ordine fecit, & convenienter decreto Hierosolymitano, quod primus ipse rogaverat. Sed venientibus Hierosolyma Judaeis ordinem hunc deseruit, & quidem φοβούμενος τὰς ἐκ περιτομῆς[?], metuens eos, qui ex circircumcisione[?] erant; ne videlicet in illorum criminationem inciderent, in qualem etiam Paulus Act. XXI. 21. inciderat. Jam primùm ergo meruit, ubi metuere non debebat, sed potiùs docere Judæos, & facti sui rationem verbo Dei & decreto Synodi consentaneam exponere. quod non semel fecisse Paulum, & alibi ipsum Petrum παῤῥησιαζόμενον[?] legimus. Metus autem erat non Dei, sed hominum, Judæorum; nec Judæorum quorumvis, sed Hierosolyma venientium, & legi addictius adhuc servientium, quos timebat ne offenderet, & ne offensi Hierosolymam reduces invidiam sibi conflarent. Hic verò metus injustus eum commovit, ut se subduceret & separaret à gentibus, ne amplius cum iis conversari, vel vesci necesse haberet. Ipsa illa ὑπάλιν[?] subductio & ἀφορισμὸς[?] separatio à gentibus, sine professione causarum, fuit tum scandalosa distractio Ecclesiæ, tum injusta coactio gentilium, ut, si cum Petro & aliis Judæis communionem optarent, Judaizandum sibi esse putarent. Et poterant sanè gentes iisdem cibis vesci, quibus & Judæi vescebantur, sed liberè, ac sine opinione necessitatis. At Petrus se propter usum ciborum seperans, opinionem necessitatis ingerebat, & si non imperio, saltem exemplo (uti S. Augustinus loquitur) docebat, gentes si vellent cum Judæis communionem habere, vel fideles Judæos excipere, Judaizare, hoc est, jugum Judæis impositum suscipere debere. Sic ergo simulatione sua & Judæos tum infirmos in errore suo de legalium necessitate confirmavit: tum firmiores, qualis Barnabas erat, ad simulationem similem seduxit: & quantum in ipsius exemplo fuit, gentilibus jugum imposuit: denique metuens summum, hoc est, scandalum Judæorum passivum, ipse in flammam incidit, & reatum scandali activi contraxit, Ecclesiámque, soluta charitatis mutuæ compage, distraxit.
units.tr: XVII. For St Peter, at Antioch, before the Jews sent by James had arrived from Jerusalem, ate with the Gentiles [μετὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν συνῇσθιε], knowing, of course, that no distinction of foods any longer held in force for the sake of religion, and that the foods God had cleansed were no longer to be regarded as unclean (Acts 10:15), and that the disciples, that is the proselytes from the Gentiles, were not to be burdened with the yoke, of which the dietary law commanded by Moses was a part (Acts 15:10, 28). Up to this point he acted in order, and in agreement with the Jerusalem decree, which he himself had first proposed. But when Jews came from Jerusalem, he abandoned this order, and indeed, fearing those of the circumcision [φοβούμενος τὰς ἐκ περιτομῆς], that is, lest he fall into their accusation, the sort of accusation into which Paul too had fallen (Acts 21:21). So at first he went wrong where he ought not to have feared, but rather to teach the Jews and to set out the reason for his deed, one consistent with the Word of God and the decree of the Synod. Paul did this more than once, and we read of Peter himself speaking boldly [παῤῥησιαζόμενον] elsewhere. But the fear was of men, not of God: of the Jews, and not of just any Jews, but of those coming from Jerusalem, who were still more addicted to serving the law, and whom he feared he might offend, and lest, once offended, they should return to Jerusalem and stir up hatred against him. This unjust fear moved him to withdraw and separate himself [ὑπάλιν, ἀφορισμὸς] from the Gentiles, so as no longer to have to associate with them or eat with them. That very withdrawal and separation from the Gentiles, made without any declaration of reasons, was then both a scandalous rending of the Church and an unjust coercion of the Gentiles, who, if they wished for communion with Peter and the other Jews, would think they had to Judaize. The Gentiles could indeed eat the same foods the Jews ate, but freely, and without any sense of necessity. Peter, however, by separating himself on account of the use of foods, was instilling a sense of necessity, and if not by command, at least by example (as St Augustine puts it), he was teaching that the Gentiles, if they wished to have communion with the Jews or to receive Jewish believers, must Judaize, that is, take up the yoke imposed on the Jews. So by his dissimulation he confirmed the Jews, then weak, in their error about the necessity of the legal observances; and he led the firmer ones, such as Barnabas, into a similar dissimulation; and as far as lay in his example, he imposed the yoke on the Gentiles. Finally, fearing the greatest thing, that is, the passive scandal of the Jews, he himself fell into the flame and incurred the guilt of active scandal, and, with the bond of mutual charity loosed, he rent the Church.

units.la: XVIII. Observavit sanè legalia quædam etiam Paulus, & infirmis factus est ut infirmus, Judæis, ut Judæus. Act. XVI. 3. XVIII. 18. XXI. 24. 1. Cor. VIII. 13. IX. 22. quod identidem veteres & novi Petri hyperaspistæ objectant. Sed dispar longè ratio est. Non enim ideo damnavit Petrum, quòd legalibus uteretur; sed quòd Judæus absentibus Judæis gentiliter viveret, hoc est, liberè cum gentibus vesceretur, iisdem verò præsentibus, dissimulata doctrina sua, ab iis se separaret, atque sic exemplo suo, cùm maxima apud Judæos & gentiles ejus authoritas flagraret, gentiles Judaizare cogeret. nec ullam gentium fidelium rationem omnino haberet, planè plane contra Hierosolymitani decreti paulò ante conditi tenorem, quod nunquam S. Paulus fecisse comperit. Sic enim cum Judæis infirmis Judaizavit, ut nec eos in errore suo confirmaverit, sed pia συγκαταβάσει[?], non sine libertatis professione usus, ceremonias quasdam eorum, quas nondum ut perniciosas odisse licebat, sed ut ἀδιαφόρως paulatim omittere conveniebat, libertate prudente, non necessitate servili, adhibuerit: nec gentes scandalo perculerit: nec vel ab his vel ab illis se separaverit unquam, odiumque adeò illud Judæorum, quo gentes tanquam fœdere indignas prosequebantur, neutiquam foverit. Unde ejus exemplo nemo unquam ad observationes Judaicas inductus legitur. quod factum exemplo Petri diserte quæritur. Verbo, ille, factus est omnia omnibus; hic solorum Judæorum rationem habuit, gentilium deposuit.
units.tr: XVIII. Paul did indeed observe certain legal practices. He became as one weak to the weak and as a Jew to the Jews (Acts 16:3; 18:18; 21:24; 1 Cor. 8:13; 9:22). The old and new defenders of Peter keep throwing this at us, and the case is far from the same. Paul did not condemn Peter for using the legal observances. He condemned him because, when Jews were absent, Peter lived like a Gentile, that is, ate freely with the Gentiles, but when Jews were present he set aside his own teaching and separated himself from the Gentiles. By this example, at a time when his authority was at its height among both Jews and Gentiles, he compelled the Gentiles to Judaize. He took no account whatever of the Gentile believers, and this was plainly contrary to the terms of the decree of Jerusalem drawn up shortly before, which Paul never violated, as we find. Paul, by contrast, Judaized with the weak Jews in such a way that he did not confirm them in their error. Through a pious condescension (συγκαταβάσει), while not failing to profess his liberty, he adopted certain of their ceremonies, which could not yet be hated as pernicious but ought gradually to be dropped as indifferent (ἀδιαφόρως). He did this with prudent freedom, not servile necessity. He did not offend the Gentiles, nor did he ever separate himself from either group, and so he never fostered that hatred of the Jews by which they treated the Gentiles as unworthy of the covenant. Accordingly, no one is ever read as having been led to Jewish observances by Paul's example, whereas the Scriptures expressly complain that this happened through Peter's example. In a word, Paul became all things to all; Peter took account only of the Jews and laid aside regard for the Gentiles.

units.la: XIX. Peccavit ergo verè Petrus, & peccavit ὑποκρίσει[?] simulatione. Sic enim peccatum ejus v. 13. definitur: Συνυποκρίθησαν αὐτῷ[?] καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ Ἰουδαῖοι[?], simulabant cum eo reliqui etiam Judæi. Neque, quod Hieronymus contenderat, simulatio isthæc fuit occultatio consilii officiosi, sed externa incauta ostensio falsæ opinionis tum de necessitate Judaismi ad salutem, tum de illicito convictu Judæorum cum gentibus, velut adhuc impuris. Quanquam enim opinionem neutram infixam animo habuit, uti ex Act. X. 28. XI.3. &c. XV.10. liquet; tamen intempestivo Judæorum Hierosolymitanorum timore occupatus desiit cum gentilibus conversari, vesci, & ab iis facto divortio Judæis solis adhæsit. Quod igitur nec animo tenuit, nec verbis vel imperio docuit, id docuit externo facto, quale eorum est, qui opinionem talem animo impressam habent. Cùm ergo opinionem infixam animo non habuerit, & tamen fecerit, quod faciunt illi, qui opinionem illam animo fovent, manifestum est, illum simulasse ob metum falsam opinionem, & simulatione ea peccasse. Si enim in humanis simulatio, uti verissimè Cicero in Lælio loquitur, tum omnium rerum est vitiosa (tollit enim judicium veri) tum amicitia repugnat maximè: quanto magis in Divinis & veritate & charitatem turbat, adeóq; vitiosa habenda est? Cúmq; Petrus & Apostolus, & Apostolorū coryphæus fuerit, facti sui exemplo ruinæ causa iis fuit, qui plurimum ei considebant, adeóque scandali activi reus. Nam & respectu Judæorum secuta est συνυπόκρισις confimulatio reliquorum Judæorum, eorum videlicet, qui paulò jam firmiores una cum Petro Antiochiæ gentium consuetudine & convictu uti cœperant; quin & ipsius comitis charissimi Barnabæ: & respectu gentilium, coactio illorum, ut Judaizarent; non quòd vel vi externa, vel imperio, minis, verbis eos ad Judaizandum impellerent, sed quòd authoritate facti sui, quod simile potentum precibus, fait species violenta jubentis, eos ad simile factum invitaret, provocaret, seduceret; si scilicet apud Judaeos in pretio aliquo esse, & Ecclesiam uniri, non distrahi, nec corpus Domini perni-ciosò schismate vexari cuperent. Quæ omnia sic merito S.Paulus v.14. interpretatur, ut &c, Petrum, & qui cum eo simulabant, asserat οὐκ ὀρθοποδεῖν πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν τῆς Εὐαγγελίου[?] non recto pede incedere juxta veritatem Evangelii, secus ac ipse alibi Hebr. XII.13. jubet τροχιὰς ὀρθὰς rectas orbitas facere pedibus, ne quod claudum est, deflectat a via, sed sanetur potius. Evangelium enim εἰλικρίνειαν καὶ ἁπλότητα[?] sinceritatem, simplicitatem, & puritatem in dictis & factis exigit. At facta illorum nec cum aliis eorundem factis, nec cum interiore & recondito sensu animi eorum, nec cum Evangelio, quod libertatis à ceremoniis legis, & justificationis, non ex operibus legis, sed ex fide Christi (quo argumento S. Paulus v. 15. 16. pugnat) præconium continet, congruebant; adeóque μετατροπὴν τῆς Εὐαγγελίου mutationem Evangelii non obscurè docebant.
units.tr: XIX. Peter therefore truly sinned, and he sinned by hypocrisy (ὑποκρίσει), that is, by pretence. His sin is defined thus in verse 13: Συνυποκρίθησαν αὐτῷ καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ Ἰουδαῖοι ("the rest of the Jews joined him in his pretence"). Nor, as Jerome had contended, was this pretence a concealment of a well-meant plan. It was an incautious outward display of a false opinion, both about the necessity of Judaism for salvation and about the unlawfulness of the Jews' fellowship with the Gentiles, as though these were still unclean. For although he did not hold either opinion fixed in his mind, as is clear from Acts 10:28; 11:3 and 15:10, nevertheless, overcome by an untimely fear of the Jews of Jerusalem, he ceased to associate with the Gentiles, to eat with them, and, having separated from them, he clung to the Jews alone. What he did not hold in his mind and did not teach by word or command, he taught by an outward act of the kind performed by men who have such an opinion fixed in their minds. Since, then, he did not have the opinion fixed in his mind, and yet did what those do who cherish that opinion, it is manifest that he pretended from fear, holding a false opinion, and sinned by that pretence. For if in human affairs pretence, as Cicero speaks most truly in the Laelius, is faulty in every matter (for it destroys the judgment of what is true), and it is especially hostile to friendship, how much more does it disturb truth and charity in divine matters, and so must be held faulty? Since Peter was an apostle, and the chief of the apostles, his example of what he did was a cause of ruin to those who relied most on him, and so he was guilty of active scandal. For in respect of the Jews there followed a joint pretence (συνυπόκρισις) on the part of the remaining Jews, namely those who by then were somewhat stronger and had begun, together with Peter at Antioch, to use the Gentiles' customs and fellowship; and also of Barnabas, his most beloved companion. In respect of the Gentiles, the pretence compelled them to Judaize, not because Peter forced them by external violence, command, threats or words, but because by the authority of his act, which, like the entreaties of the powerful, has the appearance of a violent command, he invited, provoked and seduced them to a similar act. He evidently wished that the Jews should be kept in some esteem, that the Church should be united and not divided, and that the body of the Lord should not be troubled by a pernicious schism. All this St Paul rightly interprets in verse 14, asserting that Peter and those who pretended with him did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel (οὐκ ὀρθοποδεῖν πρὸς τὴν ἀλήθειαν τῆς Εὐαγγελίου). Paul himself, elsewhere, in Heb. 12:13, bids us make straight paths for our feet, so that what is lame may not be turned out of the way, but rather be healed (τροχιὰς ὀρθὰς). The Gospel requires sincerity, simplicity (εἰλικρίνειαν καὶ ἁπλότητα) and purity in words and deeds. But their acts agreed neither with other acts of the same men, nor with the inward and hidden sense of their minds, nor with the Gospel, which proclaims liberty from the ceremonies of the law and justification not by works of the law but by faith in Christ, an argument with which Paul contends in verses 15 and 16. Thus by their conduct they plainly taught a change of the Gospel (μετατροπὴν τῆς Εὐαγγελίου).

units.la: X X. Hæc porro sic à nobis disputata sunt, non ut S.Petri lapsum ipsum exagitemus; sed partim ne excusetur, & in exemplum abeat ejus simulatio: partim ne veritas Scripturæ periclitetur, si veterum simulatam contentionem asserentium opinio vinceret. Detestanda verò est Bataneotæ, Porphyrii & Juliani sycophantia, qui ex historia contentionis illius tum S. Paulo procacitatis ob accusatum Petrum, Apostolorum principem, maculam inusserunt: tum S. Petrum hypocritæ convitio asperserunt: tum denique Scripturam ipsam talibus authoribus, & sic in dogmate suo discrepantibus nefariè prosciderunt. Non enim procacitas, sed sancta παρρησία erat, corripere publicè fratrem ab institutis Domini sui devium, publicéque peccantem, & corripiendo sic scapham appellare scapham, non insectandi studio, sed veritatem Divinam asserendi, errantem in viam revocandi, & scandalum averruncandi zelo. Nec Petrum hypocritam dicere fas est, quia simulaverit licet βραχύ τι ad breve tempus, non tamen simulavit ex malitia cordis, sed tum ex infirmitate fidei, διαλογιζόμενος[?] dubitans forte, an sicut gentilibus jugum imponendum non erat, ex Concilii Apostolici decreto, ita pariter Judæi possent gentiliter vivere: tum ex metu Judæorum Hierosolymitanorum, quos legalibus magis assuetos offendere, conversando cum gentilibus, reverítus est. cujusmodi simulatio, non habitualis, ut ita loquar, sed actualis, adeóque actio non deliberata maturo consilio, sed subita, & ex inani metu profecta, hypocritam non facit. Unde corripienti S. Paulo non restitit, sed ultro cessit, reapse demonstrans, correptionem jus-ti fuisse sibi חסד miscricordiam, & increpationem ejus שמן ראש oleum capitis fui, quo non fuerit illud fractum humíque prostratum, sed delibutum potius, & in sublime erectum, qui salutaris correptionis fructus Psal. CXLI. 5. indigetatur. Laudem ergo, non vituperium ullum justa Pauli libertas, & sancta Petri humilitas merebatur. Denique neque Scripturæ, à discordibus ita Scriptoribus consignatæ authoritas vacillat, tum quia contentionis finis conservatio illibatæ veritatis fuit: tum quia S. Petrus nec in fidei doctrina vel dogmate ullo erravit, nec erravit prædicando Evangelium, nedum Evangelium literis consignando, sed in conversatione sola humanitus aliquid passus est. Prædicatio porro & conscriptio Evangelii ex Divina inspiratione: conversatio, actiones & mores eorundem ex modo regenerationis pendebant. Inspiratio perfecta, regeneratio imperfecta fuit. Inspirati ergo & illuminati Divinitus perfectè errare non potuerunt: at regeniti in hac vita imperfectè peccare potuerunt. quod vel solum Petri ejusdem Christum abnegantis exemplum docet. Non ergo lapsus morales Sanctorum doctrinæ Divinitus inspiratæ quicquam derogant, juxta illud S. Pauli 2. Cor. IV. 7. Habemus thesaurum hunc in vasis testaceis, ut excellentia potentia sit Dei, & non ex nobis.
units.tr: XX. These things have been argued by us in this way, not to censure the fall of St Peter himself, but partly so that his pretence may not be excused and turned into an example, and partly so that the truth of Scripture is not endangered, should the opinion of those who assert a feigned dispute among the ancients prevail. The sycophancy of the Bataneotae, of Porphyry and of Julian is to be detested. From the history of that dispute they fastened on St Paul the stain of insolence for having accused Peter, the prince of the apostles; they also smeared St Peter with the charge of hypocrisy; and finally they wickedly tore Scripture itself apart, on the ground that its authors disagree in doctrine. For it was not insolence but holy boldness of speech (παρρησία) to rebuke publicly a brother who had strayed from the ordinances of his Lord and was sinning in public, and in rebuking him to call a boat a boat. This was done not from a desire to attack, but from zeal for asserting divine truth, for recalling an erring man to the right way, and for averting scandal. Nor is it right to call Peter a hypocrite, because he pretended for a little while (βραχύ τι ad breve tempus). He did not pretend out of malice of heart, but from weakness of faith, perhaps doubting (διαλογιζόμενος) whether, as the Gentiles were not to be burdened with a yoke by the decree of the apostolic council, so Jews might equally live like Gentiles; and from fear of the Jews of Jerusalem, whom he shrank from offending by associating with the Gentiles, accustomed as they were to the law. A pretence of this kind, not habitual, as I may say, but actual, and so an act not deliberated with mature counsel but sudden and arising from groundless fear, does not make a hypocrite. Hence he did not resist St Paul when rebuked, but readily yielded, thereby showing in fact that the rebuke was a kindness (chesed, [חסד]) to him, and that its sharpness was oil of the head (shemen rosh, [שמן ראש]) to him. It did not break his head and cast him down to the ground, but rather anointed him and raised him up, which is the fruit of salutary correction, as Ps. 141:5 declares. Thus the just liberty of Paul and the holy humility of Peter deserved praise, not any blame. Finally, the authority of Scripture, sealed by writers who thus disagree, does not waver. First, because the aim of the dispute was the preservation of the truth undiminished. Second, because St Peter erred neither in the doctrine of faith nor in any dogma, nor did he err in preaching the Gospel, much less in committing the Gospel to writing; he suffered something merely human in his conduct alone. Now the preaching and writing of the Gospel depended on divine inspiration, while the conduct, actions and morals of the same men depended on the mode of regeneration. Inspiration was perfect; regeneration was imperfect. Those inspired and illuminated by God therefore could not err perfectly, but those regenerated in this life could sin imperfectly. Peter's own denial of Christ alone teaches this. Thus the moral failings of the saints detract nothing from the doctrine divinely inspired, according to the saying of St Paul in 2 Cor. 4:7: We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the excellence of the power may be of God, and not of us.

units.la: XXI. Historia contentionis hujus fidei & vitæ saluberrima documenta præbet, sive S. Paulum corripientem, sive S.Petrum correptum, sive Barnabam & συνυποκρινομένης[?] Judæos, sive S. Patres de contentione hac dissidentes contemplamur. Nos præcipua eruemus.
units.tr: XXI. The history of this dispute offers most wholesome lessons for faith and life, whether we consider St Paul rebuking, St Peter being rebuked, Barnabas and the other Jews dissembling with him, or the Fathers disagreeing with one another about this contention. I shall draw out its chief lessons.

units.la: XXII. S. Paulus ingentis in causa Dei Zeli & παῤῥησίας documentum exhibet. Res erat illi cum Apostolo, & Apostolorum quidem, præsciscine dixerim, coryphæo, quem ipse prædicaverat Gal. II. 9. δοκοῦντα στῦλον εἶναι visum, seu in ea existimatione habitum, ut crederetur merito columna Ecclesiæ; haud equidem ratione potestatis vel jurisdictionis, sed ratione ministerii, & in eodem fidelitatis, constantiæ, laboris indefessi, sapientiæ ac prudentiæ, quæ in ipso, & Jacobo ac Johanne eminuerat præ aliis. Quamprimum vero ille in causa Dei cœspitare, claudicare, non incedere juxta veritatem Evangelii,errori suo implicare alios,& gentibus jugum saltem per indirectum imponere coepit,ilico cum eo S.Paulus congreditur,ei,nil reveritus furibundorum Judæorum, quos Petrus metuerat,odium,in quod ceu ignem postea incidit;resistit,eum damnat,non in angulo,non per κα-ταλαλιὰν[?]& ψιθυρισμὸν[?],sed ἐμπροσθεν[?] πάντων coram omnibus,quia coram omnibus factum coram omnibus reprehendendum censuit, omniumque reprehendi factum intererat. Docemur illustri exemplo, nos ipsos,& vitam nostram non debere tanti nobis esse, ut veritatem Evangelii prodere, vel prodentibus abblandiri velimus : licet libertate & παρρησίᾳ[?] tali hominum odia conciri constet. Nempe, Ambrosii in Psal.118. verbis utar, Zelum habere debet Dei Sacerdos, qui incorruptam servare studet Ecclesiæ castitatem. Et Phinees Sacerdos erat, & nepos sacerdotis, & filius sacerdotis. Bonus Zelus & utilis in sacerdote, præcipuè ne negligens, ne remissus sit. Vides quia Zelus Dei gratia est, qui exquirit, qui supervenit, qui se justi fundit pectori. Zelus Dei vita est. Zelum habuit Elias, & ideo ad Cælum raptus est. Zelans, inquit, Zelum domini. Et paucis multa S. Augustinus : Qui non Zelat,non amat,
units.tr: XXII. St Paul gives an outstanding example of zeal and boldness [παρρησία, parrhesia] in the cause of God. He had to deal with an Apostle, indeed with the leader of the Apostles, if I may say so with foreknowledge, whom he himself had called a pillar [δοκοῦντα στῦλον εἶναι, dokountes stylon einai] in Gal. 2:9, that is, one who was held in such esteem that he was rightly believed to be a pillar of the Church. This was not on account of power or jurisdiction, certainly, but on account of his ministry, and of the faithfulness, steadfastness, tireless labour, wisdom and prudence that stood out in him, and in James and John, above the others. But as soon as Peter began to stumble and limp in the cause of God, not walking straight according to the truth of the Gospel, entangling others in his error and laying a yoke on the Gentiles, if only indirectly, at once Paul opposed him. Paul withstood him, not fearing the raging hatred of the Jews, which Peter had feared, and into which Peter later fell as into a fire. He resisted him and condemned him, not in a corner, not by backbiting [καταλαλιά, katalalia] and whispering [ψιθυρισμός, psithyrismos], but before all [ἐμπροσθεν πάντων, emprosthen pantōn], in the presence of all, because he judged that what was done before all must be rebuked before all, and it concerned all that the deed be rebuked. We are taught by this illustrious example that we ourselves and our lives ought not to be so dear to us that we would betray the truth of the Gospel, or flatter those who betray it. It is evident that such freedom and boldness [παρρησία, parrhesia] stir up the hatred of men. To use the words of Ambrose on Psalm 118: The priest of God ought to have zeal, who strives to keep the Church's chastity uncorrupted. Phinehas was a priest, the grandson of a priest and the son of a priest. Zeal is good and useful in a priest, above all so that he is not negligent or lax. You see that the zeal of God is a grace, which seeks out, which comes upon a man, which pours itself into a righteous breast. The zeal of God is life. Elijah had zeal, and for that reason he was taken up to heaven. "Being zealous," he says, "for the Lord's zeal." And St Augustine says much in a few words: He who does not have zeal does not love.

units.la: XXIII. In S. Petro humanæ fragilitatis typus lugubris extat. Ille enim tantus Apostolus, tanta παρρησία non semel Christi causam, quin & ipsam fidelium libertatem a legali ciborum discrimine adversus ejusdem fugillatores (Act.XI. 2.3. &c.) orans, in Petra Christo fundatus Petrus, adeóque verè πεπετρωμένος[?], subitò & labitur ipse, & aliis lapsus causa exstitit. Et qui videbatur esse columna, hic arundo factus est, clarissimo argumento, partim sine gratia & manu Dei nihil nos esse, neque quenquam mortalium sibi, suisque viribus confidere posse : partim in lapsibus nostris, cùm tantas lapsorum imagines habeamus, non nimium confundi nos debere : partim denique nostrum esse, aliis labentibus non insultare, sed μετριοπαθεῖν[?] condolere, & cum iisdem à lapsu resurgentibus resurgere. Non enim, uti scite S. Augustinus in Psal. I. loquitur, cadendi exemplum (David, Petrus) propositus est, sed, si ceciderit, resurgendi. Attende ne cadas : non sit delectatio minorum, lapsus majorum, sed sit casus[?] majorum, tremor minorum. Ad hoc propositum : ad hoc scriptum est : ad hoc in Ecclesia sæpe lectum atque cantatum. Audiant qui non ceciderunt, ne cadant : audiant qui ceciderunt, ut surgant, &c.
units.tr: XXIII. In St Peter there stands a sorrowful type of human frailty. For that great Apostle, so bold [παρρησία, parrhesia], more than once pleaded the cause of Christ, and even the freedom of the faithful from the legal distinction of foods, against its mockers (Acts 11:2–3, etc.). Peter, founded on Christ the Rock and truly made firm as a rock [πεπετρωμένος, petrōmenos], suddenly slipped himself and became the cause of others' fall. He who seemed to be a pillar became a reed. This is a most clear argument: partly, that without grace and the hand of God we are nothing, and no mortal can trust in himself and his own strength; partly, that in our falls, since we have so many images of fallen men, we ought not to be overly ashamed; and partly, finally, that it is our part, when others fall, not to insult them but to feel with them in their sorrow [μετριοπαθεῖν, metriopathein], and to rise again with those who rise from their fall. For, as St Augustine well says on Psalm 1, the example set before us is not of falling (David, Peter), but of rising again if one has fallen. Take heed lest you fall: let it not be a joy to the lesser men that the greater have fallen, but let the fall of the greater be a trembling to the lesser. This is the purpose; for this it has been written; for this it is often read and sung in the Church. Let those who have not fallen hear, lest they fall; let those who have fallen hear, that they may rise, etc.

units.la: XXIV. Major fuerit laudabiliórque S Pauli corripientis Zelus, an S. Petri correpti patientia,mansuetudo,& humilitas, dubitare licet. Hic enim corripientem graviter sustinet, neque errorem defendere ullo verbo satagit. Utque tanti Apostoli modestiam mireris amplius, etiam post contentionem illam 2. Pet.III. 1s. S. Paulum ceu ἀγαπητὸν ἀδελφὸν dilectum fratrem laudat, & illum κατὰ τὴν δοθεῖσαν αὐτῷ σοφίαν juxta datam sibi sapientiam scripsisse commemorans, non obscurè à S.Paulo in hac ipsa etiam contentionis causa dicta & facta, ceu profecta à Coelesti sapientia, probat. Idque etiam Oecumenius ad h. l. his verbis praedicat: Διὰ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς Παῦλος κατηγορώσκει τῷ Πέτρῳ· καὶ Πέτρος Ἀλλὰ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς ἐγκωμάζει Παῦλον, καὶ τὰς ἐπιστολὰς σοφίας Θεοῦ ὃ χάρετ[?] μαρτυρεῖ, καὶ τὸ ἀσυ-ἐξίντας τὸν ἐν αὐλαῖς κεκρυμμένον νῦν [?] ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἀμφρέφειν ἀναβοᾷ· Paulus per epistolam condemnat Petrum; & Petrus per Epistolam laudat Paulum, & epistolas, sapientiae & gratiae plenas esse testatur, & instabiles latentem in iis mentem non intelligere, imò pervertere clamat. Similiter Chrysostomus: Παῦλος ἐπιπλήττει, ὃ Πέτρος ἀνέχεται, ἵνα ἐγκαλυμένης τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ καὶ σιγῶντ[?] εὐκολώτερον οἱ μαθηταὶ μεταθῶντες· Paulus objurgat, & Petrus sustinet, ut dum magister objurgatus obticescit, facilime discipuli mutarent sententiam. Augustinus ita concinit: Nam objurgatore suo ipse, qui objurgatur, mirabilior, & ad imitandum difficilior. Facilius est videre, quid in alio corrigas, atque id vituperando, aut objurgando corrigere, quam videre, quid in te corrigendum sit; libentérque, corrigi vel per se ipsum, nedum per alium, adde posteriorem, adde coram omnibus. Valet autem hoc ad magnum humilitatis exemplum. Si enim Petrus tantus Apostolus arguenti cessit, & corripientem dilexit, nos cum eo paria neutiquam facientes, paternos vel fraternos etiam elenchos æquo non feremus animo, errorem in conscientiæ luce convictum non libentes ejerabimus? Nimis perversè, sic iterum S. Augustinus Epist. 7. ad Marcell. scribit, amat se ipsum, qui & alios vult errare, ut suus error lateat. Quanto enim melius & utilius, ut ubi ipse erravit, alii non errent, quorum admonitu errore careat?
units.tr: XXIV. Whether St Paul's zeal in rebuking was greater and more praiseworthy, or St Peter's patience, meekness and humility when rebuked, may be debated. For Peter bore the rebuke gravely, and did not strive by a single word to defend his error. And that you may marvel further at the modesty of so great an Apostle: even after that dispute (2 Pet. 3:15–16), St Peter praises St Paul as our beloved brother [ἀγαπητὸν ἀδελφόν, agapēton adelphon], and recalls that he wrote according to the wisdom given to him [κατὰ τὴν δοθεῖσαν αὐτῷ σοφίαν, kata tēn dotheisan autō sophian], showing plainly that what Paul said and did in this very dispute, as proceeding from heavenly wisdom, was approved. Oecumenius also proclaims this on the passage in these words: "Paul by his letter condemns Peter; and Peter by his letter praises Paul, and testifies that his letters are full of the wisdom and grace of God, and cries out that the unstable do not understand, indeed pervert, the mind hidden in them" [Διὰ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς Παῦλος κατηγορεῖ τοῦ Πέτρου· καὶ Πέτρος διὰ τῆς ἐπιστολῆς ἐγκωμιάζει τὸν Παῦλον, καὶ τὰς ἐπιστολὰς αὐτοῦ πλήρεις σοφίας καὶ χάριτος θεοῦ μαρτυρεῖ, καὶ τὸ ἀστήρικτον τὸν νοῦν τὸν ἐν αὐταῖς κεκρυμμένον οὐ κατανοεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ διαστρέφειν βοᾷ]. Chrysostom similarly: "Paul rebukes, and Peter endures it, so that while the teacher, rebuked, falls silent, the disciples may more easily change their opinion" [Παῦλος ἐπιπλήττει, ὁ Πέτρος ἀνέχεται, ἵνα ἐγκαλυμμένης τῆς διδασκαλίας καὶ σιγῶντος τοῦ διδασκάλου ῥᾷον οἱ μαθηταὶ μεταθῶνται]. Augustine agrees: He who is rebuked is himself more admirable than his rebuker, and harder to imitate. It is easier to see what needs correcting in another, and to correct it by blaming or rebuking him, than to see what needs correcting in yourself; and to be gladly corrected, even by oneself, let alone by another, add by a later one, add before everyone. This serves as a great example of humility. For if Peter, so great an Apostle, yielded to the one who argued with him, and loved the one who rebuked him, shall we, by no means doing likewise, bear paternal or even brotherly reproofs with an equal mind, and not gladly cast out an error convicted in the light of conscience?
