St Augustine again writes in Letter 7 to Marcellinus: He loves himself too perversely who wants others also to err, so that his own error may stay hidden. For how much better and more useful it is that, where he himself has erred, others should not err, and by their admonition he should be free of error?

units.la: XXV. Inprimis isthæc S.Petri à Paulo correpti patientia demonstrat, non gessisse illum se pro Apostolorum Principe, Monarcha & Pontifice Oecumenico Ecclesiæ. Oecumenicus enim Pontifex ἀνυπεύθυ-νος est, & extra omnem reprehensionis, damnationis humanæ aleam. Quod Papæ gnathones agnoscunt, qui eum pro Oecumenico Pontifice venditantes, negant, ulli humano judicio eum subesse. Nam c. ad Apostolatus. Extravag. Ne sede vacante, in Glossa, hoc insignis cujusdam regulæ instar cavetur: Nemini licere Papæ dicere, cur ita facis? Et dist. 40. Papæ etiam negligentissimi & nocentissimi, innumerabiles populos catervatim secum in gehennam ducentis culpas (sic fan-cium citum est) redarguere præsumit Mortalium nullus,quod cunctos ipse judicaturus, à nemine est judicandus. Et rursus Causa. 7. 3. Nemo judicabit primam sedem justitiam temperare desiderantem. Neque enim ab Augusto,neque ab omni clero, neque à Regibus, neque à Populo judex judicabitur. Atque id ipsum novissimè Eugenius Lombardus Reg. Sacerd. p. 349. &c. aliquot Synodorum authoritate suffulcire conatur. Nec immeritò, si Supremus ille Ecclesiæ princeps est, quia talem esse, & ab inferiori reprehendi, judicari,damnari posse,ἀδύνατον[?] est. At Petrus à S.Paulo reprehensus, judicatus est. Nam hic ei in faciem restitit, eumque palam damnavit. Paulus mortalis Petri culpas redarguere præsumpsit, cùm, juxta Hieromonarchicorum scita,Papæ, ceu supremi Principis, culpas isthic redarguere præsumat Mortalium nemo. Non ergo Petrus supremus Ecclesiæ Princeps & Monarcha fuit. Et quod ipse non fuit,Mortalium nemini, Tros Rutulusve, Cæsar vel Papa suat,dare potuit.
units.tr: XXV. First of all, this patience of St Peter, when rebuked by Paul, shows that he did not carry himself as the Prince of the Apostles, the Monarch and Ecumenical Pontiff of the Church. For an Ecumenical Pontiff is unaccountable [ἀνυπεύθυνος] and outside every risk of rebuke and human condemnation. The Pope's flatterers acknowledge this, who, while puffing him up as the Ecumenical Pontiff, deny that he is subject to any human judgment. For in c. ad Apostolatus and Extravagante "Ne sede vacante," in the Gloss, this is laid down as a kind of notable rule: It is not lawful for anyone to say to the Pope, "Why do you do so?" And in dist. 40, no mortal presumes to rebuke the faults (so the saying is phrased) of popes, however negligent and harmful, who lead countless peoples in flocks with them into hell, since he who is to judge all is to be judged by no one. And again in Causa 7, q. 1: No one shall judge the first see, which desires to temper justice. For the judge shall not be judged by Augustus, nor by any clergy, nor by kings, nor by the people. And most recently Eugenius Lombardus, in Reg. Sacerd. p. 349 and following, tries to bolster this by the authority of several synods. Nor is this unreasonable, if that man is the supreme prince of the Church; for it is impossible that such a man should be rebuked, judged or condemned by an inferior. But Peter was rebuked, judged, by St Paul. For Paul withstood him to his face, and condemned him openly. A mortal, Paul, presumed to rebuke the faults of Peter, whereas, according to the decrees of the hieromonarchists, no mortal presumes to rebuke the faults of the Pope, as of a supreme prince. Therefore Peter was not the supreme Prince and Monarch of the Church. And what he himself was not, he could not give to any mortal, whether Trojan or Rutulian, Caesar or Pope.

units.la: XXVI. Male habet Hieromonarchicos hic locus. Alii enim in eo laborant,ut Petri peccatum elevent, imò cum Baronio etiam, uti supra vidimus,tollant. nullo certè cum operæ pretio. Non enim à culpa Petri, sed à reprehensione S. Pauli argumentum ducitur. Sive ergo peccatum ejus fuerit prædicationis, sive, uti rectiùs Tertullianus, conversationis vitium : sive in fide peccaverit, sive in moribus, sive grave, sive, quod Bellarminus de R. Pont. lib. I.28. statuit, veniale & levissimum fuerit, (nam Baronium negantem, quòd ullo modo Petrus peccaverit, jam supra cucurbitas lippivisse demonstravimus) certè & reprehensus, damnatus à Paulo est : & reprehensionem, damnationem admisit. quod non faciunt supremi Principes, quibus sua voluntas ratio est, & qui à nemine Mortalium se reprehendi, damnari posse, jactant. cujusmodi Oecumenicum illi fingunt. Nil ergo refert, quomodo peccaverit, dum peccaverit ; sive contra fidem, sive in conversatione. Imò si, quod certum est, tantùm in conversatione, fortius etiam argumentum stringit. Nam qui Oecumenicum Papam à nemine Mortalium reprehendi posse afferunt, ii excipiunt, si à fide sit devius, seu hæreticus. quo in casu (quem tamen evenire posse, pauci censent) reprehendi posse, largiuntur. Eò ergo receptior adversariorum sententia redit, Papam ob mores etiam corruptissimos à nemine reprehendi, damnari posse. Quomodo etiam Eugenius Lombardus loc. cit. pag. 350. Sinvessanæ Synodi authoritate probat, Marcellinum Papam thus Vestæ adolentem non potuisse nisi à se ipso judicari, allegans Melchiadis Episcopi subscriptionem : Juste ore suo condemnatus est, & ore suo suscepit anathema, quoniam ore suo condemnatus est. Nemo enim unquam judicavit Pontificem: quoniam prima sedes non judicabitur à quoquam. Et perditissimum Papam Johannem XII.flagitiis magis quàm dignitate maximum, ab Othone Imperatore throno motum, adeóque judicatum,majore Zelo quàm æquitate, cùm belli quàm juris legumque peritior esset, eandem ob causam idem Lombardus p.358. & ante eum Baronius, aliique asseruerunt.
units.tr: XXVI. This passage is troublesome to the hieromonarchists. Some of them labour to diminish Peter's sin, or even, with Baronius, as we saw above, to remove it altogether; but to no purpose worth the effort. For the argument is drawn not from Peter's fault but from St Paul's rebuke. So whether his sin was a fault of preaching, or, as Tertullian more correctly says, a fault of conduct; whether he sinned in faith or in morals; whether it was grave, or, as Bellarmine holds in de R. Pont. I.28, venial and very slight (for we have already shown above that Baronius, who denies that Peter sinned in any way, has been seeing gourds), in any case he was rebuked and condemned by Paul, and he admitted the rebuke and the condemnation. This the supreme princes do not do, for whom their own will is their reason, and who boast that they can be rebuked or condemned by no mortal, as they imagine their Ecumenical Pontiff to be. It therefore makes no difference how he sinned, provided he sinned: whether against the faith or in his conduct. Indeed, if, as is certain, it was only in his conduct, the argument is even stronger. For those who assert that the Ecumenical Pope cannot be rebuked by any mortal make an exception if he has strayed from the faith, that is, is a heretic. In that case (which few think can happen, yet they grant that it could) they allow that he may be rebuked. So the more accepted opinion of the adversaries comes back to this: the Pope cannot be rebuked or condemned by anyone even for the most corrupt morals. Eugenius Lombardus also, in the place cited, p. 350, by the authority of the Synod of Sinuessa, proves that Pope Marcellinus, who burned incense to Vesta, could be judged only by himself, citing the subscription of Bishop Melchiades: He was justly condemned by his own mouth, and by his own mouth he received the anathema, since he was condemned by his own mouth. For no one has ever judged the Pontiff, since the first see is to be judged by no one. And the same Lombardus, p. 358, and before him Baronius and others, have asserted the same reason for the most depraved Pope John XII, who, greater in his crimes than in his dignity, was removed from the throne by the Emperor Otto, and so judged, with greater zeal than justice, since he was more skilled in war than in law and the rules of justice.

units.la: XXVII. Sed aliud est (sic idem Lombardus ibid. instat) objurgare aliquem, aliud judicare. Hoc jurisdictionis est, non illud. Quicunque enim male agit, redargui potest, ut olim Nathan Davidem & Regem & Prophetam adulterii redarguit; & hodie concionatores. Quicunque ergo vas electionis es, & raptus usque in tertium Cœlum, audisti arcana verba, peccantem Pontificem, ut voles, objurga. quod etiam B. Bernhardus, aliique eodem spiritu fecerunt. Sed memento Exod. c.25. scriptum esse: Facies quoque candelabrum de auro mundissimo, emunctoria quoq; de auro purissimo. Ergo non emungat, qui aurum non est. Similia pag.525.§26.habet. Sed, ô bone, deflectis nimium tum à canonibus vestris, quibus dicitur: Papæ culpas isthic redarguere præsumit Mortalium nullus: & , in his, quæ vult, ei est pro ratione voluntas, nec est, qui ei dicat, cur ita facis? tum à verbis Apostolici textus.
units.tr: XXVII. But "it is one thing to rebuke someone, another to judge him" (so the same Lombard insists, ibid.). "This belongs to jurisdiction, not that. For whoever acts wrongly can be rebuked, as Nathan of old rebuked David, both king and prophet, for adultery"; and so do preachers today. "Therefore, you who are a vessel of election, and were caught up to the third heaven, and heard secret words, rebuke the sinning Pontiff as you wish." Blessed Bernard and others did this in the same spirit. "But remember that it is written in Exodus 25: Thou shalt make also a candlestick of pure gold, and snuffers of the purest gold." "Therefore let no one trim the lamp who is not gold." He has similar remarks at p. 525, §26. But, my good sir, you stray too far both from your own canons, which say, "No mortal presumes to rebuke the Pope's faults here," and "in those matters which he wishes, his will is his reason, and no one may say to him, why do you do so?", and from the words of the apostolic text.

units.la: S. Paulus enim non utcunque Petrum reprehendit, sed ei εἰς πρόσωπον ἀντέστη[?] in faciem restitit: & restitit ἐμπροσθεν πάντων coram omnibus: & eum κατέγνω damnavit. Etenim si judicare jurisdictionis est, quanto magis damnare? Licet autem Vulgatus verbum καταγνωσμένῳ reddat reprehensibilem: tamen negari nequit, proprie damnabilem significare, hoc est, καταγνώσεως ἄξιον damnatione dignum, condemnandum. Constat enim, ut obiter hoc dicam, Hebræis, Græcis & Latinis haud raro participia passiva non tam actum passionis, quàm dispositionem ad eam passionem significare. Ita εὐλογημένῳ pro εὐλογητός; & πειράζων, pro πειρασμός; & εἰ πεπλεσμένον ἐστί[?], pro εἰ τελεσθῆναι δυνατόν, si consummari potest. Et Hebræi vix aliter, quibus v. g. נמאס abominabilem, נבזה contemptibilem, נחמד expetibilem, נרצה amabilem, מהלל laudabilem notat.
units.tr: For St Paul did not rebuke Peter in just any way. He "withstood him to the face" [εἰς πρόσωπον ἀντέστη], "resisted him before all" [ἐμπροσθεν πάντων], and "condemned him" [κατέγνω]. For if to judge belongs to jurisdiction, how much more does to condemn? The Vulgate renders the word [καταγνωσμένῳ] as "blameworthy," but it cannot be denied that it properly means "condemnable," that is, "worthy of condemnation, to be condemned." It is well established, to say this in passing, that among Hebrews, Greeks and Latins passive participles often signify not so much the act of being acted upon as a disposition toward that passion. Thus [εὐλογημένῳ] stands for [εὐλογητός] "blessed"; [πειράζων] for [πειρασμός] "temptation"; and [εἰ πεπλεσμένον ἐστί] for [εἰ τελεσθῆναι δυνατόν] "if it can be accomplished." The Hebrews use them in much the same way: for example, [נמאס] means "abominable," [נבזה] "contemptible," [נחמד] "desirable," [נרצה] "lovable," and [מהלל] "praiseworthy."

units.la: XXVIII. Sed forte S.Paulus reprehendit Petrum, ei restitit in faciem, eum damnavit non ex authoritate, sed ex humanitate: eique S. Petrus non ex officio, sed ex modestia cessit, quemadmodum fas esse cuivis, qui aurum purissimum est, & Papam peccantem videt, eum reprehendere, Lombardus dixerat. verbo, reprehendit Paulus Petrum, ut minor majorem, & reverenter ac modestè, nequicquam interea diminuto Suprematu ejusdem. Ita Stapletonus Princip. Doctr. VI. c. 14. ita Bellarminus de Pontif. lib. I. 16 citans utérque etiam testem Augustinum & Cyprianum : ita alii. Ego quidem styli Romani distinctionem agnosco, qui S.Cerem. Eccl. R. lib.III. s. 1. quòd Romanus Pontifex nemini reverentiam facit, sic ampullatur : Quamvis solenni quadam cum Majestate Papa magnos viros ad osculum pedis suscipiat : consueverunt tamen Pontifices Cardinalibus & maximis Pontificibus privatim adventantibus, & reverentiam facientibus, quum non sint in Pontificalibus, aliquantulum caput inclinare, tanquam reverentiam reddentes : & hoc non ex officio, sed ex laudabili humanitate. Sed stylus hic Apostolicæ λεγομένης Romanæ, non Apostolicæ Divinæ & Cœlestis curiæ est. Etenim S. Paulus non simpliciter reprehendit Petrum, quod reverenter facere aliquis possit,sed ei restitit in faciem, & coram omnibus, eúmque damnavit. quia scilicet Subduxit se, Metuit circumcisos, Simulavit, Coegit judaizare, Claudicavit. quæ omnia frontem,constantiam,acrimoniam sonant, neque adeò reverentiæ,humilitatis,modestiæ,qua minor erga majorem utitur, sed authoritatis testificationem habent. qua nil dignitati Petri datum,sed religionis negotium omnibus prælatum est. Quis, amabo, sic Papæ in faciem restiterit, & restiterit coram omnibus, nisi qui vincula & mortem ipsam perpeti prius animo obfirmatus fuerit. Fuisse tamen authoritatem cum modestia,charitate, ἐπιεικεία conjunctam,ultro fateor, sed paris in parem. Tum S.Paulus sic Petro resistens, vel id fecit suo jure,vel contra officium. Hoc quis audit dicere ? Si jure resistere potuit,authoritatis igitur,non humanitatis fuit,resistere. Cúmque nemo ne quidem purissimum aurum,hoc est, ipsius Christi, ipsius S. Pauli ore & verbis usus, Papæ,Oecumenico Pontifici λεγομένῳ, jure vel authoritate resistere in faciem,nedum eum damnare audit, quis neget, sequi, Petrum non fuisse Oecumenicum Pontificem, qualem Papa se jactat ? Præterea Paulus consultò reprehensionem suam & resistentiam commemorat,qua probet,se æqualem Petro authoritate fuisse,adversus Pseudo-Apostolos, qui fidem doctrinæ illi, quam tradebat, detrahere, illum infra alios deturbando, contenderant. Si ergo Petrum reprehendit ex humanitate, non authoritate, ineptam utique rationem contexuit, qua falsam conclusionem induceret. Si B. Petro S. Paulus minor, inferior authoritate fuit, quem in finem ergo illa, cùm diceret, se putare se ipsum (μηδὲν) nihilo inferiorem fuisse summis Apostolis, 2.Cor.XI. s. & ab iis, qui existimantur aliquid, qualescunque olim fuerint, nihil sibi differre, Gal. II. 6 [?] Sedet cuivis Episcopo ita licere resistere Papæ, uti Paulus restitit Petro, non putavit Thomas Aquinas in 4. Sent. dist. 19. q. 2. art. 2. ubi factum Pauli Petrum reprehendentis dicit excedere modum fraternæ correptionis, quæ Prælatis à subditis debetur, quia id factum coram multitudine. Frustra verò Sophistæ alii æqualitatem, quam fateri coguntur, Apostolorum, officii Apostolatus, non regiminis fuisse, tricantur, quia regimen Ecclesiæ pars erat Apostolatus, cùm singuli Apostoli Ecclesiam gubernaverint: & reprehensio ipsa peccantium sive in fide, sive in moribus, non posset non pars esse regiminis Ecclesiastici. Denique Petrum Paulo cessisse non ex officio, sed ex modestia, qua fronte dicitur? Fateor equidem, humilitatis & modestiæ ejus fuisse, quòd reprehendenti indignatus non est, sed concessit. quod non majoritatem ejus, verùm animum patientem, & constantem arguit; cùm ne subditi quidem semper Prælatorum censuras æquo animo ferant. Sed ex officio non cessisse, quis sanus dixerit? Paulus enim Spiritu Dei eum reprehendit, & argumentis convicit. Si igitur cedere dedignatus esset, ipsi Spiritui & verbo Dei restitisset. Hoccine juxta, illud præter officium facturum fuisse putabimus?
units.tr: XXVIII. But perhaps St Paul rebuked Peter, withstood him to the face and condemned him, not by authority but by humanity, and St Peter yielded to him not from duty but from modesty, just as, Lombard said, it is lawful for anyone who is "purest gold" to rebuke a sinning Pope. In short, Paul rebuked Peter as the lesser rebukes the greater, respectfully and modestly, without in the meantime diminishing Peter's supremacy. So Stapleton (Princ. Doctr. VI, c. 14) and Bellarmine (de Pontif. I, 16), each citing Augustine and Cyprian as witnesses, and others. I indeed recognise the distinction of the Roman style, which in the Caerimoniae Ecclesiae Romanae (III, s. 1) says, "that the Roman Pontiff shows reverence to no one," and puffs it up thus: "Although the Pope, with a certain solemn majesty, receives great men to kiss his foot, the Pontiffs are accustomed, when Cardinals and great prelates visit them privately and pay them reverence, though they are not in pontifical dress, to bow the head a little, as returning the reverence; and this is done not from duty, but from praiseworthy humanity." But this style belongs to the so-called Roman court of the apostles, not to the divine and heavenly court of the apostles. For St Paul did not simply rebuke Peter in a way that anyone might do with respect, but "withstood him to the face, and before all," and "condemned him," namely because Peter "withdrew himself," "feared the circumcised," "dissembled," "compelled [the Gentiles] to Judaize," and "was led astray." All these words sound of boldness, steadfastness and sharpness, not of the reverence, humility and modesty which a lesser person uses toward a greater, but they carry the mark of authority. Nothing was granted to Peter's dignity; rather the cause of religion was placed above everyone. Who, pray, would so withstand the Pope to his face, and withstand him before all, unless he had first steeled his mind to endure chains and death itself? I freely admit that authority was joined with modesty, charity and gentleness, but it was authority from one equal to an equal. Then, when St Paul withstood Peter in this way, did he act by right or contrary to duty? Who would hear anyone say the second? If he could withstand by right, then it was of authority, not of humanity, that he withstood. And since no one, not even the purest gold, that is, one who uses the very mouth and words of Christ himself and of St Paul, dares to withstand the so-called Oecumenical Pontiff to his face by right or authority, much less to condemn him, who would deny that it follows that Peter was not the Oecumenical Pontiff that the Pope boasts himself to be? Moreover, Paul deliberately records his rebuke and resistance in order to prove that he was equal to Peter in authority against the pseudo-apostles, who had contended that the faith of the doctrine he preached should be taken away from him, by pushing him below the others. If, then, he rebuked Peter from humanity rather than authority, he devised a senseless argument, one that would lead to a false conclusion. If St Paul was inferior to St Peter in authority, why then did he say that he thought he was in no way (μηδὲν) inferior to the chief apostles (2 Cor. 11), and that those who seemed to be something, whatever they were of old, made no difference to him (Gal. 2:6)? Thomas Aquinas did not think it was allowed for any bishop to withstand the Pope in the way Paul withstood Peter (in 4 Sent. dist. 19, q. 2, art. 2), where he says that Paul's act of rebuking Peter exceeds the measure of fraternal correction, which is owed to prelates by their subjects, because that act was done before a crowd. Other sophists vainly twist the equality of the apostles, which they are forced to admit, into being one of "apostolic office," not of "governance," because governance of the Church was part of the apostolate, since each of the apostles governed the Church; and the very rebuke of sinners, whether in faith or in morals, could not but be part of ecclesiastical governance. Finally, with what face is it said that Peter yielded to Paul not from duty but from modesty? I admit indeed that it was a mark of his humility and modesty that he was not offended at the rebuke but yielded to it; this shows not his inferiority but a patient and steadfast mind, since not even subjects always bear the censures of prelates with an equal mind. But who of sound mind would say that he did not yield from duty? For Paul rebuked him by the Spirit of God and convicted him with arguments. If, then, he had disdained to yield, he would have resisted the Spirit itself and the Word of God. Shall we think that he would have acted in accordance with the one and against duty in the other?

units.la: XXIX. Neque seorsim citati Patres sentiunt. Non enim illi simpliciter majorem à minore, sed priorem à posteriore correptum dicunt, quia S. Petrus prior, S. Paulus posterior vocatus est. Sic planè Augustinus Epist. 19. ad Hieron. Rarius & sanctius exemplum Petrus posteris præbuit, quo non dedignarentur à posterioribus corrigi: quàm Paulus, quo confidenter auderent minores majoribus pro defendenda veritate, salva charitate, resistere. Minores ergo illi posteriores sunt, non officii & potestatis, sed vocationis, donorum, ordinis gradu. Ita contra Donat. lib. II. 1. & Comm. ad h. l. semper posteriorem Paulum appellat. Cyprianus difertior ad Quintum: Nec Petrus, inquit, quem primum Dominus elegit, & super quem ædificavit Ecclesiam suam, cùm Paulus de circumcisione postmodum disceptaret, se vindicavit, aut arroganter aliquid vel insolenter assumpsit, ut diceret, se primatum tenere, & obtemperari à novellis & posteris sibi potiùs debere. En novellum, posterum! Primatum verò vocationis, ordinis inprimis intelligunt. Optimè Ambrosius in Epist. ad Gal. c. 2. Quis eorum auderet Petro, primo Apostolo, cui claves Regni Cœlorum Dominus dedit, resistere, nisi alius talis, qui fiducia suæ electionis, sciens se non imparem, constanter improbaret, quod ille suo consilio fecerat? En, alius talis, non impar!
units.tr: XXIX. Nor do the Fathers cited separately think otherwise. For they do not say simply that the greater was rebuked by the lesser, but that the "earlier" was rebuked by the "later," because St Peter was called first and St Paul later. Augustine says this plainly in Epist. 19 to Jerome: "Peter gave a rarer and holier example to those who came after, by not disdaining to be corrected by those who came after him, than Paul gave, by which those lesser ones dared with confidence to resist their greater ones in defending the truth, while preserving charity." Those lesser ones, then, are later in the order not of office and power, but of calling, gifts and rank. So too in contra Donat. II, 1 and in his commentary on this passage he always calls Paul the "later." Cyprian is more explicit in ad Quintum: "Nor did Peter, whom the Lord first chose, and upon whom he built his Church, when Paul afterwards disputed with him about circumcision, claim the right to himself, or arrogantly or insolently assume anything, so as to say that he held the primacy and that the new and later ones ought rather to obey him. Behold, a new one, a later one!" But they understand the primacy chiefly of calling and of rank. Ambrose excellently says in his commentary on Galatians, c. 2: "Who of them would dare to resist Peter, the first apostle, to whom the Lord gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven, unless another such man, who, trusting in his own election, knowing that he was not unequal, constantly disapproved what that man had done by his own counsel? Behold, another such man, not unequal!"

units.la: XXX. Unum addo, historia contentionis jugulari etiam δογ-μαπικὴν[?] ὑπολήψιν[?] illam de infallibilitate Papæ in jure, & fallibilitate in facto ; quam moderatiores tuebantur hactenus. Erravit sane Petrus in facto, non lapsus est (uti recte Tertullianus adv. Marc. lib. V. 3.) in perversitatem Divinitatis, id est, in subversionem articulorum fidei. Nihilominus separationis, subductionis, simulationis suae facto & Judæos & gentes in errorem doctrinæ, quem etiam Nazaraei erraverunt, duxit, ut legem necessariam esse putarent. Non potuisset enim, uti Augustinus Epist. 9. scribit, cogere Judaizare, nisi sic egisset, tanquam etiam post Domini adventum legalia nec stabilia saluti forent. Nihili ergo distinctio illa est, ubi de doctore ἀναμαρτήτῳ[?] agitur. Nam & facta doctoris docent.
units.tr: XXX. I add one further point. The history of this dispute also cuts the throat of that dogmatic opinion [δογματικὴν ὑπολήψιν] of the Pope's infallibility in law and his fallibility in fact, which the more moderate defended until now. Peter certainly erred in fact, but he did not fall (as Tertullian rightly says, Against Marcion, book V, ch. 3) into a perversion of the Godhead, that is, into the overthrow of the articles of faith. Nevertheless, by his act of separation, withdrawal and dissimulation, he led both Jews and Gentiles into the error of doctrine that the Nazarenes also fell into, so that they thought the law was necessary. For, as Augustine writes in Epistle 9, he could not have compelled them to Judaize unless he had acted as though the legal observances were still binding for salvation even after the Lord's coming. That distinction therefore counts for nothing when we are dealing with an infallible teacher [ἀναμαρτήτῳ]. For a teacher's deeds also teach.

units.la: XXXI. S. Petrus se ὑπεστέλλε[?] & ἀφωρίζε subducebat & separabat à gentibus fidelibus, eoque nomine gravem S.Pauli reprehensionem, imo & damnationem incurrebat. Docemur, neminem quicquam debere eligere in cultu, in quo non possint aut teneantur omnes idem facere ; neque fas esse, se separare à fidelibus propter ritus, ceremonias, aliasque causas non necessarias. Pharisaismi hæc fibra est, dicentium : קרב אליך לא תגש בי כי קדשתיך Accede ad te, ne tangas me, quia Sanctus tibi sum, vel sanctior te sum, Esaj LXV.5. Qui pridem corpus Christi fœdè depasci cœpit, & hodieque depascitur, cùm non desinunt οἱ ὑποστολῆς[?] filii,(Hebr.X.39.) qui novæ cujuspiam sanctitatis typho inflati, ex alto fratres quosq; despiciant, judiciis temerariis infestent, suas iisdem leges severè imponant, adversus eos digitum extendant,(Esaj.LVIII.9.) [illegible, ~12 letters] nescio quam, certè sine duce & luce Deo, commendent ; eos, quos convertere, & quorum regenerationi inservire debuerant, procul à se arceant ; recte posita moveant ; odio improborum tesseram societatis frangant ; denique παλιγγενεσίας Ecclesiæ, quæ quidem bonis omnibus per media Divinitus ordinata curæ esse debet, prætextu sic Zizania ex agro Domini eradicare conentur, ut tritico ipsi, tot Sathanæ furoribus, tot tempestatibus obnoxio, novas insidias struant, ne dicam, quantum in ipsis est, illud una cum Zizaniis eradicent. Tanti scilicet non erat excusssse jugum Antichristi, nisi vel novum jugum hominum talium subire, vel eorundem communione, & suavissimo illo communionis fructu, quem David Psal. CXXXIII. 1. his verbis : Quàm bonum, quàm jucundum est, fratres habitare una, decantavit, carere velimus ! Ruminanda hic piis & placidis à S. Augustino Lib. III. contra Parmen. cap. 1,2. dicta puto. ubi sic inter alia ille : Cum pia ratio & modus Ecclesiastica disciplina veritatem spiritus in vinculo pacis maximè debeat intueri: quod Apostolus sufferendo invicem præcipit custodiri, & quo non custodito medicina vindicta non tantùm superflua, sed etiam perniciosa, & propterea jam nec medicina esse convincitur: illi, qui non odio iniquitatum alienarum, sed studio contentionum suarum infirmas plebes, jactantia sui nominis irretitas, vel totas trahere, vel certè dividere affectant, superbia tumidi, pervicacia vafani, seditionibus turbulenti, ne luce veritatis carere offendantur, umbram rigidæ severitatis obtendunt: & quæ in Scripturis S. salva dilectionis sinceritate, & custodita pacis unitate, ad corrigenda fraterna vitia, moderatiori curatione, fieri præcepta sunt, ad sacrilegium schismatis, & occasionem præcisionis usurpant.
units.tr: XXXI. St Peter withdrew [ὑπεστέλλε] and separated [ἀφωρίζε] himself from the believing Gentiles, and on that account incurred the grave rebuke, indeed the condemnation, of St Paul. We are taught that no one should choose anything in worship that not all can or are bound to do in the same way, and that it is not lawful to separate oneself from the faithful on account of rites, ceremonies, and other unnecessary causes. This is the fibre of Pharisaism, which says: "Keep away from me, do not touch me, for I am holier than you, or I am more holy than you" [קרב אליך לא תגש בי כי קדשתיך], Isaiah 65:5. He who long ago began to foully feed upon the body of Christ, and still feeds upon it today, since the sons of "those who shrink back" [οἱ ὑποστολῆς] (Heb. 10:39) do not cease. Puffed up with the conceit of some new holiness, they look down from on high on their brothers, harass them with rash judgments, impose their own severe laws on them, and point the finger at them (Isaiah 58:9). [illegible] They commend I know not what, certainly without God as guide and light. Those whom they ought to have converted and served in their regeneration they keep far from themselves. They stir up what has been rightly settled. In hatred of the wicked they break the token of fellowship. Finally, under the pretext of uprooting tares from the Lord's field, they try to root out the regeneration [παλιγγενεσίας] of the Church, which ought to be the care of all good people through the means God has ordained. So they set new snares for the wheat itself, which is exposed to so many frenzies of Satan and so many storms. I will not say that, as far as they are concerned, they would uproot it along with the tares. Clearly it was not such a great thing to shake off the yoke of Antichrist, unless we are willing to undergo a new yoke of such men, or to do without their fellowship and that most sweet fruit of fellowship which David sang of in Psalm 133:1 in these words: "How good and how pleasant a thing it is, brethren, to dwell together." I think the sayings of St Augustine here are to be pondered by the pious and calm, in Book III against Parmenian, chapters 1 and 2, where among other things he says this: "Since a pious reason and method of Church discipline ought above all to regard the truth of the Spirit in the bond of peace, which the Apostle commands us to keep by bearing with one another; and when this is not kept, the remedy of vengeance is not only superfluous but harmful, and for that reason is shown to be no remedy at all. Those who, not from hatred of others' sins but from zeal for their own contentions, aim either to draw whole weak communities, ensnared by the boasting of their own name, or at least to divide them, swollen with pride, crafty in obstinacy, turbulent with seditions, put forward the shadow of stern severity, so that they may not be seen to lack the light of truth. And they usurp for the occasion of schism and the sacrilege of separation those precepts of Scripture which are given for correcting a brother's faults by a gentler treatment, with the sincerity of love preserved and the unity of peace kept."

units.la: XXXII. Barnabæ & Judæorum σωαπαχθέντων[?] simul abreptorum, ut cum Petro simularent, facinus illustri documento est, quanta illustrium exemplorum vis sit. Nam tanti Apostoli Petri exemplum etiam in malam partem valuit. Scilicet quod exemplo magno fit, id etiam jure fieri homines putant. Validiora, uti sapienter Leo I. Serm. de Laur. monet, sunt exempla, quàm verba, & plenius est opere docere, quàm voce. Sicut verò arbor magna cadens minores multas corripit: sic viri magni & in Ecclesia eminentes, qui reliquorum columnæ esse debebant, lapsi semel plures secum abripiunt, transversòsque avehunt. Hæc magnis exemplis labendi cautela esse debet.
units.tr: XXXII. The carrying away of Barnabas and the Jews, who were swept along together [συναπαχθέντων] so as to dissemble with Peter, is an illustrious proof of how great the force of illustrious examples is. For the example of so great an Apostle as Peter had force even for evil. Clearly men think that what is done by a great example is also rightly done. "Examples," as Leo I wisely warns in his sermon on Laurence, "are stronger than words, and it is fuller to teach by deed than by voice." Just as a great tree in falling crushes many smaller ones, so great men eminent in the Church, who ought to be the pillars of the rest, once they fall carry many others with them and sweep them away headlong. This must be the caution against falling through great examples.

units.la: XXXIII. Sed & tristis Barnabæ ejusdem & Judæorum lapsus, non esse ad conscientiæ securitatem satis præsidii in virorum piorum exemplis, ostendit. Parum enim apud judicem Paulum Barnabæ vacillanti, & inter Judaismum ac Christianismum quasi claudicanti patrocinii in Petri, summi quantumvis inter Apostolos nominis, exemplo fuisset. Licet enim acriori reprehensione dignior fuerit Petrus, quàm Barnabas, quia suo huic exemplo nocuit, nihilo tamen excusatior Barnabas fuit, quia alieno exemplo abripi se passus peccavit. Nempe cùm non omnia omnium facta imitanda esse constet, difficile est tum judicare, quænam ex iis in exemplum trahenda sint, quæ non, quia fieri potest, ut quod à viro pio factum est, non fuerit recte factum; vel quod recte factum est, imitandum non sit: tum applicare aliorum exempla ad res & actiones nostras, propter circumstantiarum incertitudinem, quæ cùm infinitæ varietatis sint, humanas etiam actiones variare infinitis modis possunt. Habeant sanè exempla ad morum institutionem, vitæque emendationem ingens momentum. At regula vivendi sola Dei voluntas in verbo ejus patefacta est.
units.tr: XXXIII. The sad fall of Barnabas himself, and of the Jews, also shows that the examples of pious men are not enough protection for the security of conscience. For the example of Peter, however great his name among the Apostles, would have been of little defence to Barnabas before the judge Paul, who was wavering and, as it were, limping between Judaism and Christianity. Although Peter deserved a sharper rebuke than Barnabas, because he harmed others by his example, Barnabas was none the more excusable, because he sinned by allowing himself to be carried away by another's example. Indeed, since it is agreed that not all the deeds of anyone are to be imitated, it is hard (1) to judge which of them are to be taken as examples and which not, since it can happen that what a pious man did was not rightly done, or that what was rightly done ought not to be imitated; and (2) to apply the examples of others to our affairs and actions, because of the uncertainty of circumstances, which, being of infinite variety, can vary human actions in infinite ways. Examples certainly have great weight for the training of morals and the amendment of life. But the sole rule of living is the will of God, revealed in his Word.

units.la: XXXIV. Denique S. Patrum de contentione Apostolorum conflictatio supra expositá hunc usum habet, ut noverimus, judicium rerum Divinarum, & interpretationem authenticam verbi Divini non ab hominibus, sed à solo Deo in verbo suo loquente repetendam esse. Quanta enim, quæso, in Ecclesia Augustini & Hieronymi nomina sunt? Illi tamen in explicanda contentione Apostolorum infestis signis collisi diu, in eundem sensum conspirare non potuerunt. Fuit tum Augustinus juvenis: Hieronymus senex & emeritus, hoc sibi Epist 13. Aug. vindicans, quòd juxta vulgare proverbium bos lassus fortius figat pedem. Habuit sua castra Hieronymus: habuit Augustinus. Ille Origenem, Didymum, Apollinarem, Eusebium Emisenum, Theodorum Heracleotem: hic Cyprianum, Ambrosium in suis numeravit. Non caruit aculeis disputatio. In aciem venerunt argumenta ultro citróque. Nec Augustinus Hieronymo, nec Hieronymus Augustino cessit. Inter Hieronymi simulationem, & Augustini veritatem nutantes conscientiæ quem tranquillitatis portum habebunt, si non Verbi Divini & rationum pondera, sed Patrum authoritas in arce collocatur? In hoc ipso ergo argumento S. Augustinus ipse à Patribus ad Apostolum provocavit, sic Epist. 19. ad Hieronymum scribens: Flagitas à me, ut aliquem saltem unum ostendam, cujus in hac re sententiam sim secutus, cùm tu tam plures nominatim commemoraveris, qui te in eo, quod adstruis, præcesserunt, &c. Si quæras, quid hinc senserit noster Ambrosius, quid noster itidem Cyprianus, invenies fortasse, nec nobis defuisse, quos in eo, quod affirmamus, sequeremur. Quanquam tantummodo Scripturis Canonicis hanc ingenuam debeam servitutem, qua eas solus ita sequar, ut conscriptores earum nihil in eis omnino erràsse, nihil fallaciter posuisse non dubitem. Proin cùm quæro tertium, possem quidem, ut arbitror, facilè reperire, si multa legissem; veruntamen ipse mihi pro his omnibus, imò supra hos omnes Apostolus Paulus occurrit. Ad ipsum confugio, ad ipsum omnes, qui aliud sentiunt literalibus suis tractatibus, provoco, ipsum interrogans interpello & requiro.
units.tr: XXXIV. Finally, the conflict of the holy Fathers over the dispute of the Apostles, set out above, has this use: that we should know that the judgment of divine things and the authentic interpretation of the divine Word are to be sought not from men but from God alone, speaking in his word. For how great, I ask, are the names of Augustine and Jerome in the Church? Yet they, clashing for a long time with hostile standards in explaining the dispute of the Apostles, could not agree in the same sense. Augustine was then young; Jerome was old and retired, claiming for himself, as Augustine's Epistle 13 says, that according to the common proverb "a tired ox plants its foot more firmly." Jerome had his camp; Augustine had his. Jerome counted among his own Origen, Didymus, Apollinaris, Eusebius of Emesa and Theodore of Heraclea; Augustine counted Cyprian and Ambrose among his. The dispute lacked no stings. Arguments came into battle back and forth. Neither Augustine yielded to Jerome, nor Jerome to Augustine. Between Jerome's dissimulation and Augustine's truth, what harbour of tranquillity will wavering consciences have, if the weight not of the Word of God and of reasons, but the authority of the Fathers, is placed on the citadel? In this very matter, therefore, St Augustine himself appealed from the Fathers to the Apostle, writing thus to Jerome in Epistle 19: "You demand that I show at least one whose opinion in this matter I have followed, since you have named so many by name who went before you in what you maintain, etc. If you ask what our Ambrose thought, or what our Cyprian likewise thought, you will perhaps find that we too were not lacking those whom we might follow in what we affirm. Yet I owe this frank servitude only to the canonical Scriptures, so that I alone follow them in such a way that I do not doubt their writers erred in nothing and put nothing falsely. Therefore when I seek a third, I could indeed, I think, easily find one if I had read much; but for all of these, and above all of these, the Apostle Paul meets me. To him I flee; to him I call all who think otherwise in their own literal treatises, questioning him, asking him and seeking him."
